title: Promoting equity in research funding requires collaboration now more than ever
summary: In contested and cautious times, cross-sector working is needed to push EDI work forward. Rachel Van Krimpen explains what this looks like in the context of research funding
full_text:
Across the sector, work focused on equity has become more contested, more scrutinised – and, for some colleagues, more personally risky.

In that context, collaboration isn’t just beneficial, it’s becoming essential. Not only can cross-sector working produce stronger, more credible outputs, it can also distribute risk, offering a degree of protection and collective confidence to those taking this work forward.

For research funding, this presents a particular challenge. Decisions about who gets to apply, how opportunities are allocated, and what counts as fair process are increasingly shaped by scarcity, complexity, and institutional caution.

In the current global climate around EDI, there is a growing sense that sticking one’s institutional head above the parapet carries an unwelcome level of risk, while working collectively can help build a little more bravery into the system.

Collaboration under pressure

One response to this challenge has been to create spaces where institutions can step briefly out of competition and work collectively on shared problems. In early 2024, the University of Oxford convened a cross-sector forum bringing together research funders and universities to explore how recommendations from its work on equity in research funding might be taken forward in practice. The premise was simple: what might become possible if institutions paused competition long enough to rethink how it operates?

What followed was not just a set of outputs, but a sustained experiment in collaborative working under pressure. Two priorities emerged quickly from this work: inclusive demand management, and the use of positive action in research funding and careers. Neither is new, but both have become harder to navigate in a funding landscape defined by scarcity, heightened scrutiny, and institutional caution.

Demand management – limiting the number of applications that can be submitted – forces organisations into choices about who gets to compete at all. Positive action, meanwhile, offers one route to addressing persistent inequalities but is frequently constrained by legal uncertainty and a high degree of perceived risk.

In both cases, the challenge is not simply technical. It is shaped by judgement, confidence, and the conditions in which decisions are made. It was here that the value of working collectively became most visible – and where trust, flexibility and care proved as important as shared priorities.

Lessons learned

First, collaboration helped to distribute and make sense of risk. Questions around legality, fairness, and proportionality are often navigated cautiously within individual organisations, particularly where reputational stakes feel high. Working across institutions created space to test assumptions, surface shared concerns, and build more confident, risk-aware approaches. What might feel difficult or exposed in one organisation became more manageable when approached collectively.

Second, it enabled a level of openness that can be hard to sustain locally. In a more contested environment, some colleagues feel unable to share examples of practice or to be publicly associated with EDI work. A cross-sector setting, grounded in trust and shared purpose, made it easier to acknowledge uncertainty, learn from partial or imperfect approaches, and draw on a wider base of experience than any single institution could offer. Even within these collaborative communities, some contributors chose not to be named on outputs – noting fear of potential repercussions on them personally.

Third, it created the conditions for sustained progress, rather than isolated effort. Momentum in this kind of work depends on more than goodwill. Regular engagement, shared ownership, and visible progress between meetings helped turn intention into output. Crucially, this was underpinned by a realistic understanding of scope: the aim was not to resolve inequity in research funding in its entirety, but to produce practical tools that organisations could use within their own contexts.

What emerged from this process were two substantive, sector-facing resources: guidance on inclusive demand management, and a framework for positive action in research funding and research careers. Their significance lies not only in their content, but in what they represent; an example of how collaboration can make progress possible in areas where individual institutions might otherwise hesitate.

At a time when work on equity is becoming more contested and more cautious, the risk is not just that progress slows, but that it quietly stalls altogether. If acting alone increasingly feels untenable, then collaboration is not just a route to better practice, it is a condition for making progress at all. The challenge now is not whether we value collective action, but whether we are prepared to invest in it as a sustained and necessary way of advancing EDI in higher education.

The author would like to thank Claire Edwards, Strategic Research Development Manager (Research Growth) at the University of Nottingham, Ipshita Ghose, Head of Research Strategy and Development at the University of Birmingham, Fiona McClement, University Lead for EDI at the University of Edinburgh, and Faye Robinson, Associate Director Research Development at the University of York.

title: Where does the international student deficit really lie?
summary: International students are often treated as financial assets rather than pedagogic partners. Sumeya Loonat sets out four lenses for moving beyond the deficit model
full_text:
In 2019 I moved from teaching English language at De Montfort University into my current role more broadly supporting international students in our business school.

The last seven years have opened my eyes to the actual lived realities of international students’ experiences of studying in the UK, to see those experiences rather more holistically than merely through the lens of their linguistic proficiencies.

As I learned and developed in my own understanding of, and approaches to, the international student experience, I came to appreciate the importance of such learning and development for all staff involved in teaching and supporting international students. The importance of ensuring that all staff are equipped with the skills and mindset essential to support the enhancement of this sometimes underserved area of the higher education experience became clear.

I found myself engaged in frequent conversations with colleagues across our sector which returned repeatedly to the same point: an acknowledgement of a lack of practical approaches underway to challenge what can be seen as the “international student deficit model,” and to develop ways to address the issues underlying it.

This was because – as I came to see – one of the more deleterious clichés of British higher education has been the common assumption that international students can be defined by a series of deficits, by the assumption that they lack English language abilities, critical thinking skills, and familiarity with British academic conventions.

The wrong assumption

As academics we’re of course trained to recognise and interrogate preconceptions promulgated without the evidence necessary to support them.

Yet this one somehow relentlessly persists. We’re all aware that our understanding of the world can be led dangerously astray by stereotypes – and indeed, in this case, a tired old stereotype will start to melt away as soon as we look at what’s actually taking place.

When we come to examine the shortcomings of the international student experience, it emerges that the most significant area of deficit may not in fact lie with the students themselves at all.

It may instead lie in the approaches taken by that colleague who lacks an appropriate understanding of their students’ educational histories or with an institution that provides its staff with minimal professional development to support students with different educational and cultural backgrounds. It may lie with a curriculum that treats western academic conventions as universal, incontrovertible and sacrosanct or assessment frameworks that were never designed with diverse learners in mind.

Partners, not pennies

In partnership with colleagues from the University of Wolverhampton, the University of Manchester and Manchester Metropolitan University, our QAA-funded Collaborative Enhancement Project has charted these possibilities and has proposed a route towards a more ethical and expansive model of international student pedagogy.

We started by convening a series of workshops involving staff from our four institutions to find out what was really going on in our approaches to international students and how we might improve them. We created these spaces to share good practice – from ways to design inductions to the co-creation of assessment briefs – and involved a broad range of colleagues, from leaders of our international teams to senior academic practitioners, coming together in a spirit of constructive candour to explore the differences we might make.

One point that was particularly striking from the outset was that the participants in these workshops consistently identified the ways in which institutions frame international students as financial assets rather than pedagogic partners.

Unprompted by our facilitators, the term “cash cows” was used directly and repeatedly by members of staff – colleagues stressed that they found this framing at the same time accurate and deeply uncomfortable.

It seems inevitable that the financial logic of their recruitment shapes the conditions in which international students arrive, the speed at which they are expected to integrate, the support made available to them, and the ways in which their presence, expectations, and needs are communicated to academic staff.

We’ve reached the conclusion that when an institution that recruits students as a part of its financial strategy and then tasks individual educators with the consequences of that strategy is producing structural injustice, not a pedagogic problem.

When an institution recruits a student from overseas, taking significant fees, giving them a place that may shape their future and making promises about the education and experience they will receive, it incurs an obligation that goes well beyond logistics. What is required – and this is the fundamental obligation which that institution places upon itself – is that the provider ensures a sustained, resourced, and embedded commitment to the conditions in which that international student can genuinely thrive.

Four ways forward

This has led us to emphasise an urgent pedagogical and ethical imperative to reframe UK higher education’s traditional “international student deficit” narrative.

In order to address this, we’ve developed four interconnected lenses for examining both institutional provision and individual practice. We’ve done this by seeing these issues through the positioning and construction of the international student, the epistemological centring of western academic conventions in curricula, a reflexive examination of the assumptions underpinning pedagogic practice, and an interrogation of the structural conditions that make inclusive practice impossible. This includes workload pressures, large class sizes, late arrivals, a lack of professional development and the financial logic of mass international student recruitment.

Published alongside an audit toolkit and a guide to inclusive practices, our project has also proposed a set of principles designed to underpin ways to support staff in enhancing the international student experience.

Before you teach, recognise who is in the room as individuals with histories, knowledge, and perspectives, not as a category defined by fee status or visa type

When a student appears to struggle, ask where the deficit actually lies – honest diagnosis is the precondition for honest intervention

Act where you can, and name what constrains you: inclusive practice requires both individual commitment and institutional change

Centre the voices of international students: decisions about curriculum, pedagogy, and support should be informed by the actual experiences of the students they are intended to serve

The duty of care towards international students does not begin at induction, it begins when recruitment promises are made

See what international students bring rather than what they lack, and to build the structures that allow those contributions to be recognised and valued

It’s only by valuing all of our students as unique individuals and unique learners, rather than as agglomerations of income-generating assets and recognising the richness of diverse perspectives and experiences that all our students bring that we can begin to build properly equitable and effective learning processes. And in doing so we can share the benefits underpinned and enriched by all those who contribute to the learning experience.

That’s an important lesson for educators, institutions, and policymakers.

And also, perhaps, for all those who in the mass media and public life who have sought to represent the presence of international students in the UK as a problem – or, at best, as an increasingly essential income stream – rather than as a rich cultural and intellectual resource we should endeavour most effectively to utilise, support, sustain, and celebrate.

This project has crucially been a collaborative effort, and as such has highlighted the vital importance of collaboration and co-creation in this space. It has recognised that a hostile environment – one which presumes problems and deficits – helps no one, and that partnership and belonging benefits all.

title: Some students arrive to find the door to belonging already shut
summary: Radhika Sharma has followed five students' experiences from the Global South and finds belonging is a design choice that the sector keeps getting wrong
full_text:
We tend to talk about belonging as something students grow into.

Give them a term or two, a couple of societies, and a friendly flat mate, and they will settle. The five students I spent a year listening to described something closer to chasing a bus that has already pulled away from the stop.

I followed five students from the Global South at a Scottish university across one academic year. They kept journals in whatever form suited them, prayers, lists, fragments, long entries written at two in the morning, set down on their own terms without me deciding what counted. I did not want their experiences filtered through my questions before they had a chance to name them in their own words.

What they produced was not a list of grievances. It was a quietly life account of how a university decides who gets to belong, and when.

The belonging window

The sharpest pattern was the student could see from inside their own year.

The opening fortnight of term carries an enormous social load. Friendships form easily because everyone is equally adrift, society sign-ups happen in a rush, group chats assemble overnight, and the cost of saying hello to a stranger is briefly almost nothing.

I came to think of this as a belonging window. It opens for everyone at once and closes for everyone at once. The real question is who can be in the building while it is open.

Roma, an undergraduate from Nigeria, arrived three weeks into term. Her visa, her flights and her family circumstances did not rearrange themselves to fit the university calendar. By the time she reached her first lecture the benches had their regulars, the cohort chat was already trading in-jokes she could not follow, and the easy welcome of week one had set into something she now had to break into from the outside.

She had dreamed of arriving. She arrived to find the place had carried on without her. And this is not a story about one student, and that is the point. Late arrival is produced, and it is produced unevenly.

Visa backlogs, the price of an international flight, caring responsibilities that cannot be paused, programmes that start off cycle, all of these land hardest on the students our access statements say we most want to reach. The window shuts at the same moment for everyone. Only some students ever had a fair chance of getting through it.

Coming into focus

Once you see the window, other things sharpen into view.

Every student in the study described a constant background calculation about how much of themselves was safe to show.

Shiv, a postgraduate from India, arrived from a classroom culture built on respect for expertise into British seminars that reward interruption and pushback. He could read the new rule easily enough. Playing it while also wondering whether his accent had already cost him the benefit of the doubt was a second job running underneath the first.

Erica, a doctoral researcher from Ghana, weighed every seminar contribution as a Black African woman in a room that did not extend her the authority that it extended others without thinking.

For Shiv there was a further layer, the careful management of an LGBTQ+ identity that was celebrated in some campus spaces and dangerous to reveal near the co-nationals who kept in touch with home. And it all runs at the same time as the actual studying rather than in some separate, quieter hour.

Filling in the gaps

What moved me the most was what students built when the institution came up short.

Erica had a church that expected her each week, a diaspora group that swapped recipes and hardwon advice about the university’s own systems, and a community organisation that took her research seriously.

Nya’s days were held together by the religious society and the rhythm of Ramadan, which gave her a structure the rest of campus rarely offered. Roma found the chaplaincy, warm and undemanding, where a hot chocolate came with no requirement to explain herself first. We usually file these under cultural preference, the nice extras that sit beside the real support. I think that reading is backwards.

Students built these circuits because the official ones were hard to reach or not matched to their lives, and the circuits worked because they offered the one thing formal provision so often withholds, which is repetition.

Somewhere you can return to and be known without translating yourself at the door. Read properly, these student-made systems are not just curiosities but the clearest blueprint we have for what our own support keeps missing.

It really is the little things

The other side of this is how little it took to turn a student’s year around.

A tutor saying a contribution was interesting, right after it had been delivered in a shaky voice and a strong accent. A laptop loan finally approved after weeks of unexplained refusals. These sound minor, and that is exactly why they matter.

For someone who has been bracing to be heard as less capable before they have even spoken, a small signal that their voice carries knowledge rather than getting in its way is a genuine redistribution of authority. Repeated across a year, these moments gather into something that starts to feel like standing.

So what would it mean to take this seriously?

It would mean designing for repetition rather than pouring everything into the first fortnight, so that the chances to connect, to be recognised and to find support are spread across the whole year. It would mean building a real welcome for students who arrive off cycle, instead of leaving them to reconstruct week one alone in week four. It would mean recognising and resourcing the student communities already doing the heaviest belonging work, rather than admiring them from a distance. And it would mean clearer support pathways so that a student does not need “insider” knowledge of which door to knock on to reach help they are entitled to.

Underneath all of it the students were not just having experiences for me to interpret. They were theorising their own lives, in lines like being present is not the same as belonging. That is knowledge, produced from inside conditions no outside observer can reach, and it deserves to be treated as knowledge rather than as raw feeling waiting for an academic to make sense of it.

Belonging is not a personality trait some students happen to have and others lack.

It is something we hand out, on a schedule, through a hundred small design choices about timing, tone and who gets recognised. The good news buried in these journals is that if we are the ones distributing it, then we are also the ones who can distribute it more fairly. We just have to stop treating the door as if it opens itself.

title: Civic universities need collective approaches to bring students and long-term residents together
summary: In some residential areas, universities’ civic agendas can ring hollow. Kate Seymour presents a collaborative project which aimed to co-create hope in Fallowfield
full_text:
For decades, Fallowfield has provided a home for new arrivals in Manchester.

An historic connection with the city’s higher education institutions means many newcomers are students. Mention Fallowfield to residents, past and present, and it frequently evokes fond recollections and nostalgic affection. If you have ever lived in Manchester, you may well have stories of your own.

But everything in Fallowfield is not as rosy as such nostalgic sentiments may suggest. Walking around its streets, there are signs everywhere of neglect and disrepair. Landlords seeking to maximise occupancy levels have partitioned rooms and built extensions across gardens and into the roofs and basements of their multi-occupied properties. This has led to over-crowding within the neighbourhood, mounting pressures on resources, and the concreting over of green spaces. The high street overflows with takeaways and vape shops, but many other needs are significantly under-served. The situation is particularly acute in the area known historically as Fallowfield Village, which largely coincides with the postcode district M14 6.

It would be easy to blame students for Fallowfield’s ills. Data shows that the suburb has the densest student population in the city. Some streets have over 85 per cent student residents, with only a handful of owner occupiers remaining. Residents suggest litter, anti-social behaviour and late-night noise are perennial problems, echoing common criticism of other heavily “studentified” areas across the UK.

Yet our Collective Inquiry research project, carried out during 2025 and focusing specifically on the M14 6 area, demonstrates that this demographic imbalance is harming not just permanent residents but also students.

Housing lies at the heart of the problem. While many students have the misfortune of living in sub-standard yet over-priced housing, the knock-on impacts are felt throughout the community. Substantial monetary outflows (to absentee landlords amongst others) reduce the ability and will of others to invest in, and commit to, the neighbourhood.

In recent decades, the number of permanent residents has shrunk dramatically, depriving the area of those who might otherwise perform the often invisible civic work that is vital for a well-functioning neighbourhood. Indeed, after only a year, even students frequently move on. Dense impermanent and transient populations make the neighbourhood a target for criminals, giving rise to frequently repeated safety concerns.

Civic universities and the hyperlocal

The situation in hyperlocal neighbourhoods like Fallowfield is a problem for the growing ambitions of civic universities. Historically, universities were focused on the on-campus lives of their students. But in recent years, promoting student welfare has increasingly entailed actively supporting students to navigate off-campus issues as well, such as cost-of-living pressures, the private housing market, safety concerns, and health, wellbeing and belonging.

Meanwhile, there is increasing demand that universities deliver positive social impact: not only in far-flung corners of the world, but also on their doorstep. The five Manchester-based universities have united behind a recently refreshed civic university agenda, aiming to deliver impact for the city region in four key priority areas: opportunity and prosperity, health and wellbeing, culture, and environment.

They are undoubtedly key anchor institutions in the city, creating thousands of local jobs, delivering significant economic and social impact, and helping make Manchester a highly desirable place to work, study and live. Both Manchester Metropolitan University and the University of Manchester independently contribute more economic value (GVA) to the city region than the city’s two leading football teams combined.

Nevertheless, there remains a persistent gap between high-level civic ambitions and the lived realities of hyperlocal neighbourhoods. Organisations like the United Kingdom Town and Gown Association (UKTGA) have long highlighted the importance of long-term, place-based neighbourhood partnerships that recognise students as residents and citizens within shared local spaces.

Yet too often, civic university activity is still articulated at the scale of city regions, innovation districts or strategic partnerships, without translating into sustained relationships with the communities living alongside campuses and student populations. As a result, the civic agenda can ring hollow in long-suffering areas like Fallowfield, where residents’ prevailing lived experience of university neighbours may be a significant negative impact on their quality of life.

Overcoming fragmentation

The Collective Inquiry was a co-created project based on the principle of researching with rather than on communities. The research team consisted of over thirty participant-researchers including long-term residents, staff and students from two universities, representatives from the local authorities and other partner organisations. From the beginning, permanent residents and students were at its heart. We took a multi-perspectival approach to better understand the challenges facing the M14 6 neighbourhood using a variety of techniques, including a walking methodology, a systems mapping exercise, and follow-up interviews. Whilst the team did not agree on everything, we were able to identify points of convergence to focus on shared goals.

Our report identified long-term fragmentation as a key driver behind the problems faced here. Over many decades, as a result of deliberate policy decisions, governance gaps, and unintentional oversights, Fallowfield has fallen between the cracks.

Institutionally, responsibility for proactively supporting and managing student populations in local neighbourhoods sits uneasily between public authorities and universities. Partnerships are typically focused on symptom management, such as minimising the disruption of the annual student move in/move out.

Politically, the area sits between three wards and two constituencies. Ward-level data reporting can serve to obscure demographic characteristics of areas like M14 6 where boundaries meet. Meanwhile local councillors, who are elected to represent residents of their own ward, have struggled to tackle deeply engrained challenges across ward boundaries. As a result, the approach to M14 6 is all-too-often reactive and piecemeal.

Socially, there is a lack of cohesion across the whole community. There are strong student communities as well as strong, if depleted, communities of permanent residents. Yet these worlds rarely overlap and interactions that occur tend to be negative. Conflict between individuals takes the place of collective contestation of the systemic harms impacting both groups: a dynamic not dissimilar to many other polarised societal contexts.

We want to recognise that many groups and individuals have worked hard over the years to overcome these challenges. For example, residents’ groups undertake the grinding work of monitoring and objecting to planning and licensing applications. Community-led projects, often supported by the council’s local neighbourhood teams, seek to restore pride in the area. Recent examples include new public murals, the volunteer-led restoration of the Shakespearean Garden, and Clifton WEB’s tree-base planting. The small Manchester Student Homes Team, supported by excellent student ambassadors, work hard to support local residents and students attending both centrally located universities. Yet in all cases, resources are tight and volunteer initiatives rely on too few people to be sustainable.

Meanwhile, opportunists – many operating in a poorly regulated for-profit housing market – have taken advantage of gaps in governance to extract large profits from Fallowfield and the students who call it home. This has outwardly reduced a distinct neighbourhood with a rich, diverse heritage to a generic student area, reinforced by long-standing cultural narratives and institutional communications. Far from the “vibrant neighbourhoods” championed by the local authorities, fragmentation has left Fallowfield run-down, neglected, imbalanced and unsustainable.

Co-creating hope

In March this year, we held a roundtable to share the outcomes of the Collective Inquiry and discuss how to implement its recommendations. Hosted in Ladybarn Community Hub, the event brought together over 50 participants representing key actors in M14 6: the universities, local authorities, elected officials, student unions, long-term residents, police, landlords, renters and others. To the best of our knowledge, this was a truly historic gathering: the first time that so many key stakeholders have come together to focus on collectively building a better future for the neighbourhood in the neighbourhood.

[image]

In the spirit of the Collective Inquiry, the roundtable was co-led by permanent residents and students. Side-by-side, speakers argued for a strategic, holistic, inclusive and data-informed approach to the neighbourhood. One resident spoke movingly of the experience of ostracism from a neighbourhood in which her family had lived for three generations. Student representatives shared lived experiences of poor housing, exploitative landlords and the need to be valued and supported as citizens of the city. Both groups proposed constructive and complementary measures to drive up the quality of housing, improve communications and develop a place-identity for the benefit of all those who live, work and study in Fallowfield.

We then welcomed three senior respondents: University of Manchester president Duncan Ivison, Manchester Metropolitan University academic registrar Joe Rennie, and Councillor Gavin White, Executive Member for Housing and Developing. We were delighted with their positive responses and commitments to a new shared partnership approach.

The next step is to create a new taskforce for M14 6, co-chaired by students and residents, which will work to improve data, housing standards, communications and place-making. We anticipate that the taskforce will both address long-standing challenges in this neighbourhood and provide a new collaborative model for managing ever-growing student populations across the city region. It will address GMCA priorities particularly around housing, with the potential to connect to innovations like the Good Landlord Charter, and support the implementation of additional HMO licensing. It is our hope that this work will begin to overcome decades of fragmentation.

As participants left the roundtable, many commented on the hope that they now feel for the neighbourhood’s future. This reaction suggests that initiatives like the Collective Inquiry can help to better ground civic universities in place.

At the hyperlocal level, universities need to not only honestly recognise and collectively address negative impacts, but also allow themselves to be impacted by those with whom they share space. This project shows the power of slow, inclusive, co-created and democratically organised research to connect people around shared concerns and empower diverse communities to develop inclusive solutions. We are profoundly grateful for the time, dedication and (often unpaid) work of everyone who has supported this project. The hope now is that the taskforce will drive forward the changes that Fallowfield urgently needs to become a unified, peaceful and sustainable neighbourhood.

This article was written in collaboration with members of the Collective Inquiry research team, whose contributions significantly shaped its development: Helen Aczel, M14 6 resident, founder and former co-ordinator of the South East Fallowfield Residents Group and coordinator of Clifton WEB; Heather Alberro, Lecturer at the University of Manchester; Joel Dowson, Greater Manchester Student Partnership Manager; Kattie Kincaid, M14 6 resident and project lead for the Shakespearean Garden; Jason Lee, University of Manchester graduate and former chair of the Manchester Student Renters Union; and Rosalyn Marron, Senior Lecturer at Manchester Metropolitan University.

We would also like to thank Cooper Healey, Manager at Manchester Student Homes, for her helpful comments on an earlier draft, and colleagues at Manchester Metropolitan University, the University of Manchester and Manchester City Council for their ongoing support.

title: The high-street university: why the neoliberal trap is devaluing the UK degree
summary:

The post The high-street university: why the neoliberal trap is devaluing the UK degree appeared first on HEPI.
full_text:
This blog was kindly authored by Rayhan Abdullah Zakaria, Senior Fellow of the Higher Education Academy (SFHEA).

The UK Higher Education sector is currently broken. It is, as touched upon in a HEPI report by Edward Venning, obsessed with ‘Global Rankings’ and ‘Recruitment Targets’. We measure our success by the volume of international student deposits and the square footage of our new glass-fronted business schools. However, beneath this polished exterior lies a systemic crisis. We have reached a tipping point where the neoliberal view of higher education has successfully reduced the ‘Grand Ivory Tower’ to a mere ‘High-Street Retailer’. We are no longer selling the pursuit of truth; we are selling a commodity. And as any economist will tell you, when you commoditise something, you inevitably cheapen it.

The luxury handbag culture

Under the Neoliberal Economic Trap, the ‘Successes’ of a university is measured by recruitment rates and the student’s financial ability to pay, rather than their cognitive ability to create new knowledge. We have entered a Badge-Mill culture, selling MBAs, MScs, and even PhDs like luxury ‘handbags’ bought from Western prestige brands.

The student has become a ‘consumer’ and the degree has become a ‘product’ to be purchased rather than a journey to be earned. This focus on the ‘student as a fee-payer’ has eroded the very identity of the University. We have lost the roots of why we are here: to act as the conscience of society and the engine of original thought. Think of the giants like Abdus Salam, Chandra Bose, Hayat Sindi, Einstein, or Newton, they were recruited for their intellectual capital, not their liquid capital. They did not need a high-net-worth bank statement to prove their ‘financial viability’ before being allowed to wonder, question, and create.

Symptoms of structural decay

The recent news of the King’s College London and Cranfield University merger is a primary symptom of this malaise: two giants – in terms of impact in the field of knowledge – joining forces to maintain ‘market share’ in a world that increasingly views education as a transaction. This is not a merger of academic ambition, but a defensive huddle against a failing economic model.

We see the human cost of this commoditisation in the redundancies sweeping the sector, such as the University of Nottingham placing 2,700 staff members at risk. When the ‘product’ doesn’t sell as expected, the ‘factory workers’ – the academics – are the first to be sacrificed. This volatility is the direct result of a system that views knowledge as a retail export rather than a public good.

We need to find ways to subsidise and support the ‘Hayat Sindi’s’ of the 21st century who are currently being priced out of the market by high-street tuition rates. (For context, Professor Hayat Sindi at the University of Cambridge revolutionised the field of biotechnology, as well as being the first-ever female scientist originating from the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia.) If universities move toward a self-sufficient model, where revenue is generated by patents, spin-offs, and industrial problem-solving, we can afford to be choosy. We can stop chasing student fees and start chasing student genius.

The pivot: a self-sufficient model

We must reclaim the university as a place where new knowledge is created, not just where existing textbooks are recycled for a fee and we do this by:

Decoupling from Fee-Reliance: We must diversify income streams through direct industrial partnerships, patent-holding, and social enterprises that generate revenue from the application of knowledge, not just the teaching of it. By becoming ‘Innovation Hubs’ that take equity in the solutions we discover, mirroring the highly successful venture-equity models seen at the University of Oxford’s Oxford Science Enterprises, Imperial’s White City Innovation District, or the University of Cambridge’s Cambridge Enterprise, we can end the fragile dependency on international recruitment rates. Even outside the Golden Triangle, institutions like the University of Strathclyde have proven that deep-rooted industrial partnerships can fundamentally diversify a higher education institution’s income stream.

Knowledge over badges: We must de-emphasise the ‘prestige’ of the institution and re-emphasise the impact of the graduate. We need to move away from the view of the degree as a buyable asset for the global elite. An academic qualification should be a testament to a person’s ability to synthesise and challenge, not a certificate of their financial status.

Direct industrial problem-solving: Instead of generic ‘off-the-shelf’ degrees, universities should generate income through high-level consultancy and bespoke research for industry. We should be selling solutions to global problems, climate tech, AI ethics, and engineering, directly to the sectors that need them.

Returning to our roots

If we continue down the current path of neoliberal commoditisation, we risk reaching a point of ‘zero-value equilibrium’ where everyone holds a Masters but no one possesses the ability to think. We don’t need more students with large bank balances; we need more students with large questions.

It is time to stop being a high-street retailer. It is time to stop selling badges and start fostering the brilliance that will define the next century. We must return to our roots and ensure the University remains the engine of original thought, independent of the market’s fickle whims.

title: ‘I want to be ripped to shreds’: writers flock to MFAs - but does it breed elitist literature?
summary:
Thousands of budding US novelists enlist in courses each year, hoping to gain credentials that often influence who gets published

Thomas Pynchon was known to avoid the press and refuse interviews. There are only two official photographs of the Gravity’s Rainbow author available publicly – one taken at high school, the other during his time in the navy. full_text:
Thomas Pynchon was known to avoid the press and refuse interviews. There are only two official photographs of the Gravity’s Rainbow author available publicly – one taken at high school, the other during his time in the navy. He is the embodiment of the American image of a great writer: a mysterious recluse who works in a turret alone.

These days, the writerly lone wolf is more a myth than it is a reality. Most of today’s celebrated authors are trained in the profession and their qualification is the MFA (master of fine arts). Percival Everett received his from Brown, Chimamanda Ngozi Adichie studied at Johns Hopkins University, and Jhumpa Lahiri went to Boston. Great writers, now, are less rare animals discovered in the wild and more elite thoroughbreds, meticulously trained and set up for the race ahead.

An MFA is a graduate programme in a creative subject – like painting, sculpture or, in this case, writing. There are courses taught in fiction, poetry or nonfiction. They usually take two years and cost between $10,000 for a low-residency programme and upwards of $80,000 a year for a full-time programme. The vast majority of programmes are in the US: the non-profit group Poets & Writers list more than 250. That’s thousands of budding novelists enlisting each year, most expecting to graduate with a complete manuscript.

The MFA format was pioneered by the Iowa Writers’ Workshop which, founded in 1936, was the first MFA in creative writing. Led for years by the poet Paul Engle, it has spawned great writers such as Flannery O’Connor and Marilynne Robinson. Iowa’s teaching style is based around workshops where students sit around a table and discuss their peers’ work, guided by a professor. In theory, the pressurised environment of the workshop makes students examine work analytically – not emotionally – with an emphasis on craft, rather than content. Supposedly, it is this rigorous and supportive environment that strengthens a writer’s aesthetic muscles for a long and successful career ahead. In reality, workshop can be hell.

In Lena Dunham’s Girls, everyone in Hannah’s Iowa Writer’s Workshop is toxic, including Hannah. After she insults her cohort at a party, pigeonholing each “type” of writing, she is torn to shreds in workshop, told that her story “trivialises” abuse. When she tries to defend herself, the workshop leader cuts her off and tells her to wait until everyone’s finished with their critiques.

In the introduction to Dismantle: An Anthology of Writing from the Vona/Voices Writing Workshop, Junot Díaz writes about nearly dropping out of Cornell because of the “almost lunatical belief” by his predominantly white cohort “that race was no longer a major social force”. Workshop is not necessarily a safe space separate from the prejudices and conflicts of the outside world; rather it can be a crucible where these are intensified.

This backstabbing atmosphere is taken to demonic extremes in Mona Awad’s novel Bunny: Samantha, the outcast of a writing workshop, infiltrates its beautiful elite – wealthy girls nicknamed “the bunnies” – only to find they spend their time performing satanic rituals, creating Frankenstein men from rabbits and then murdering them.

I experienced some of those dynamics, without quite as much rabbit homicide, during my MFA at New York University (NYU). I remember one workshop where someone presented their writing and no one said a thing, apart from me. The awkwardness was palpable as I nattered on, struggling for new things to pick out in the extract. No one stepped in to save me. People looked pointedly at the table or their laps. The girl next to me was Googling places to eat. Even the workshop leader ran out of things to say.

I found out later that this collective silence was an act of revenge: the student who was being workshopped hadn’t written a feedback letter to anyone that term. After that workshop, their detailed letters quickly resumed.

While the idea that the workshop is de facto a magical, hermeneutic space where mediocre writing turns into something great is a lie, it can be a tool. For the most part my workshops were generous and generative spaces where people read plentifully and with grace. A writer who is forced to confront her work regularly through the eyes of others must think about what it is she wants to write and why, and this inevitably leads to writing that is more thoughtful and ambitious. Of course, learning who to listen to is a skill in itself.

Casting a dream literary dinner

Looking at the NYU MFA faculty is like casting your dream literary dinner: Jeffrey Eugenides, Jonathan Safran Foer, Katie Kitamura, Garth Greenwell, Brandon Taylor, Joyce Carol Oates, Ocean Vuong, Sharon Olds, Claudia Rankine, Valeria Luiselli, Hari Kunzru, Parul Sehgal: the list goes on. Surely, under the warmth of such suns, you will become a star?

There is a rigour and insight a great writer can bring to your work. Anelise Chen, writing for the Rumpus, describes Zadie Smith as “the most precise teacher I have ever had … she puts our writing on an overhead projector and line-edits each page”.

Joyce Carol Oates is known for her strict style. One of her students once described her crossing through the first several pages of a story and asking: “What’s the point?” I commiserated with him, but he looked at me and said: “No, that’s what I want. To be ripped to shreds.”

It is true: much of my first novel, Jean, can be attributed to the advice of my teachers. Jean is set in 1976 in a hippy, rural boarding school for boys with “problems”, and is a broken love story between Jean and a wealthier student, Tom. When I arrived at NYU, I had a bad first draft that spanned 80 years and 12 narrative voices. After Booker-shortlisted novelist Brandon Taylor (who received his MFA from Iowa) coached me in the value of long scenes, my characters unravelled, others fell away and my novel started to take shape. It was in Garth Greenwell’s (who also received his MFA from Iowa and was the 2025 PEN/Faulkner award for fiction recipient) class where I learned how to write the sex. Jonathan Safran Foer (who does not have an MFA) read three drafts of the manuscript and made me think about how meaning tracks on a large scale; Booker-shortlisted Katie Kitamura (who does not hold an MFA) helped me navigate moments of intense emotion through restraint; and Pulitzer winner Jeffrey Eugenides (who received his MFA from Stanford) made me consider how my sentence construction fit into the broader schema of my work.

But it is also true that relying too much on the opinion of one person is dangerous. There were classes where I obsessively counted how many times, if at all, my professor said “good”, deaf to their other advice and critique. Towards the end of my MFA, I became susceptible to, and afraid of, the slightest suggestion. My friends and I cried after our supervisions (private meetings with faculty mentors), whether good or bad, simply because we were exhausted by how much we cared. However wonderful a teacher is, the truth is no professor can live up to your wild expectations. What you want is their exclusive attention, all the time. If I’m being honest, I wanted to climb into their brains or find some way of turning them into Borrowers so I could carry them around with me all the time. It might not be healthy.

At most MFAs professors read work a few times a term. Some treat supervisions as pastoral check-ins; others use the time to analyse what you’ve written. Often, they might forget things or rearrange. They are busy and replies take time. You’re not the only person demanding their insight. They may even say things with which you disagree. After all, the suns are themselves only human.

But do all these MFA programmes produce a certain kind of MFA novel? In 2009, critic Mark McGurl published The Program Era: Postwar Fiction and the Rise of Creative Writing in which he argues that “the rise of mass higher education” is “something we should account for first if we are to understand postwar literature”. McGurl argues there is a recognisable kind of fiction produced by the MFA programme and offers a detailed taxonomy of the kinds of writing it produces: “technomodernism” for postmodern writers such as Pynchon; “high cultural pluralism” for writers engaged in the representation of identity through modernist tropes such as Philip Roth and Toni Morrison; and “lower-middle-class modernism” with minimalist and maximalist subcategories for writers such as Raymond Carver and Oates.

J Robert Lennon, writing in Salon, is more straightforward when he dismisses programme fiction as, “mannered, conservative and obvious”. And Anelise Chen takes this one step further when she writes: “let’s face it, any of us would rather read an amazing story dictated by an illiterate drunk than a boring ‘in the house and around the yard’ drama expertly crafted by a well-turned Program writer.”

What seems to be the consensus is that an MFA teaches you style as opposed to soul. A focus on craft, on how to write, creates automatons who can turn a good phrase, but whose writing is stripped of something essential. Pulitzer prize-winning Robert Olen Butler, interviewed by Edward J Delaney for the Atlantic, sums it up: “creative-writing students, who are typically trained almost exclusively in craft and technique […] don’t know the first thing about [being an artist].” Jo Ann Beard told me she could recognise an Iowa Writer’s Workshop graduate anywhere. There was something honed, particular and controlled in the writing. Perhaps the imprint MFAs have had on fiction feels more forceful at a time when the gulf between literary and popular fiction has never been wider. Do MFAs guard the ivory tower of literary fiction while “untrained” writers produce popular fiction for the masses? Or more generously, do MFAs protect a dying art?

While it is true that spending hours in a classroom under the influence of certain teachers can create similarities in style among a cohort, in my classes students submitted widely: magical realism, noir, historical, auto-fiction. They had epic aspirations.

Yet there is a sense that contemporary fiction conforms to a similar style. Is this because MFAs encourage that? I’m not sure. Or is it rather the influence of narrow trends, which force certain books into the public eye at certain times. That many of the most popular authors today have MFAs, and that those novels might have a similar style or focus on a similar subject is a bit like saying fire engines cause fires.

My MFA course at NYU has produced many great writers in recent years: Raven Leilani, Maggie Millner, Lillian Fishman. That becoming a published writer is even a possibility creates untold pressure in MFAs. Even if they deny it, everyone hopes they might be the next big thing. But this is not the case. I sold my book during the programme, but by that point I had been working on it solidly for four years and wrote seven drafts from scratch. The advance was not life-changing. There’s an argument for an MFA as the gateway to first-time publication, but it’s not a guarantee. In June 2024, I graduated and moved back to London. Six months later, I was diagnosed with breast cancer. I spent the next year either in hospital or on the sofa. During the MFA I was driven by an unrelenting force. I complained about being stressed and my demanding workload with the scorn of the healthy. It was only when I couldn’t even look at a computer screen that I reflected on what the previous two years had taught me.

Writing a novel is hard and takes a long time and they’re not all going to be the same. Ottessa Moshfegh’s first book, McGlue, which she wrote during her Brown MFA, is an experimental work about a drunken 19th-century sailor. Afterwards, she published the noir-like Eileen, the maximalist My Year of Rest and Relaxation and the esoteric Lapvona. Her books are so different it would be hard to call any one of them programme fiction.

What the MFA has done is formalised something that historically hasn’t been. But why do we give more licence to art students learning a craft? Spending hours life drawing is a bit like spending time doing detailed character studies. The problem is the commercialisation of fiction: who decides what gets published and why.

You can drive yourself crazy trying to say exactly how an MFA influences writing, and whether it is worth it. The truth is, an MFA isn’t a magic pill. It’s much harder to pastiche a style than you think; spending hours on anything takes stamina. Doing an MFA puts you in a rigorous environment for several years where, hopefully, you can learn how best you write. As Everett put it in Brown’s alumni magazine: “Brown allowed me to really just be who I am and just work.”

title: Montessori learning is being shut down at Leah’s school – is a push towards ‘explicit instruction’ to blame?

full_text:
Michelle’s year 8 daughter, Leah*, has been in and out of hospital since birth with complex medical issues, and Michelle says flexible learning through a Montessori program has allowed her to keep up with school.

She says the Montessori stream at their nearby public school in Victoria has taken a lot of anxiety out of her daughter’s education, due to its “self-directed learning”.

“My daughter has a lot of time in hospital and if you’re coming back to a mainstream school you’re feeling that anxiety because the kids are up to chapter 16 and you don’t know what the topic is and it’s really hard to come back in,” Michelle said.

“With Montessori it’s self-directed learning, so wherever you’re up to you don’t have to compare yourself to the kid next to you … that fits perfectly for her, she just slides back in there like she’s always been there the entire time.”

But the Montessori stream, which runs from years 7 to 9 at the Templestowe College public school north-east of Melbourne, is being phased out. Michelle, who helped found the Coalition for Choice in Public Schools group, believes it is because of the state government’s policy forcing all public schools to teach via explicit instruction, a different learning model to Montessori’s.

What is explicit instruction?

Explicit instruction, which has gained traction in recent years, has become a flashpoint in a long-running culture war over educational theory.

The method is teacher-led rather than student-led learning, where the educator will explain a lesson in small chunks, demonstrate the skill and then ask the student to model it. It’s different to “inquiry-led learning”, where students discover information for themselves.

Education experts say explicit instruction an important method but not the whole solution to improving learning in schools.

In 2024 Victoria announced the Victorian Teaching and Learning Model 2.0, which mandated explicit instruction in collaboration with the Australian Education Research Organisation (Aero), a contentious body that has heavily focused on that model.

Under the VTLM 2.0, all Victorian government schools must fully embed the policy in their teaching by 2028 and in some instances will “include retiring approaches and practices that do not align with the VTLM 2.0”.

Since the policy was announced, two Montessori streams in Victorian public schools and one Steiner stream have been shut down or phased out. There remains one Montessori stream in Victoria and five Steiner.

The state education department said it is up to Victorian public schools whether they offer an alternative program such as a Montessori, Steiner or International Baccalaureate stream. In a letter to a parent, seen by Guardian Australia, the department says it “has not issued any directive in relation to the ‘retirement’ of alternative curricula”.

Mark Powell, director of education services at Montessori Australia, said Aero and the VTLM 2.0 model promulgate a one-size-fits-all approach to teaching, which doesn’t work for all students.

“In June 2024 the government launched VTLM 2.0, a mandatory teaching framework with a hard 2028 deadline [with] very explicit language allowing for the retirement of non-aligned programs … and then the closure of three programs in the last two years, it looks like a policy design,” he said.

“Montessori is an evidence-based methodology. It’s been internationally recognised over the last century and it’s been proven by many peer reviewed studies to be highly effective for diverse learners including those with neurodivergence.”

At the same time, the federal government has buried a damning independent report into Aero, which the body claims would cause it “serious reputational harm”.

The education department blocked Guardian Australia’s freedom of information request for the report by KPMG, commissioned by Labor, because it could risk damaging relations between the states and commonwealth.

Aero objected to the release, according to the FoI rejection, saying it would “undermine trust in the quality of evidence Aero generates, with a risk that educators and other stakeholders would cease using its resources”.

It said the release could cause “serious reputational harm to Aero … damaging its ability to engage with partner jurisdictions”, as well as harm Aero’s relationships with members, “undermining its ability to fulfil its functions”.

De-professionalising teaching

Alex Bacalja, a senior lecturer who works in initial teacher education at Melbourne University, said teachers, schools and academics had criticised Aero because of its heavy focus on explicit teaching, and accused it of moving decision making and experience from educators to bureaucrats.

“Because Aero claims to know the best methods of teaching, and communicate that knowledge through departments of education, teachers are no longer allowed to decide what is best for the students in front of them at any one time, a bureaucrat has decided that for them … it aims to de-professionalise teaching,” he said.

“It’s like a bureaucratic department telling brain surgeons how to do brain surgery.”

Bacalja was involved in consultation sessions organised by KPMG during the audit.

“I thought there would be a balance of those people who mostly supported Aero’s work and others far more critical. It was all critical,” Bacalja said. “I know colleagues who attended other consultation sessions with KPMG who shared similar stories.”

The Greens’ education spokesperson, Penny Allman-Payne, said it was “appalling” the report was hidden from the public.

“Aero is meant to be Australia’s national education evidence body and yet they won’t provide to teachers, other educators and school leaders, the evidence of the report into how well they’re functioning … I think that’s pretty appalling.”

The former public school teacher said she had heard criticism from educators and researchers that Aero “takes a very narrow focus on which evidence they use and look at”, and heard other concerns that some of the resources on the website were “insulting” because they were so basic and would have been covered in university.

The federal government is working towards absorbing Aero, the Australian Curriculum, Assessment and Reporting Authority (Acara), the Australian Institute for Teaching and School Leadership (AITSL) and Education Services Australia (ESA) into a new “teaching and learning commission”.

The department, in its FOI response, said some education ministers claimed the release of the audit could “prejudice ongoing discussions” about the new commission, but Allman-Payne said the KPMG report should be released because of the new body.

“Information in that report is going to be critical to any decisions that are made … a good process would involve everybody understanding what’s gone well with the bodies that they want to amalgamate and what hasn’t.”

* A pseudonym has been used to protect identity

title: How parents and pupils took on 'cruel', 'authoritarian' schools - and won
summary: Discipline at an academy trust went too far - parents, pupils and former teachers tell BBC Panorama.
full_text:
To avoid getting into trouble, 14-year-old Amelia says she decided to stop drinking water at schoolso she would not need the toilet.

Her school, Camborne Science and International Academy in Cornwall, had introduced strict disciplinary policies, which included limiting toilet visits during classes, according to pupils and former teachers.

New discipline rules were implemented when the school was taken over in January 2024 by the Athena Learning Trust, which runs six secondary schools in Devon and Cornwall.

Amelia's mother, Kayley, believes these strict policies resulted in her daughter becoming ill from a series of serious infections caused by not drinking.

Hundreds of parents, including Kayley, have campaigned against the way Athena run its schools.

Across Devon and Cornwall, there have been public meetings, school-gate protests and online petitions. Local MPs and councillors have also backed concerned parents.

The opposition to Athena now appears to have paid off - with the trust announcing last month that it was planning to disband and transfer all its schools to other trusts.

It said that trustees had "listened carefully to feedback" and recognised the "clear need for change".

BBC Panorama has spoken to nearly 100 pupils, parents and former teachers from Athena schools, who say levels of discipline went too far. Many pupils and parents queued to talk to us at two town hall meetings we arranged.

The way the schools had been run was "authoritarian" and "cruel", some said.

"You're constantly scared you're going to do something wrong," one student with ADHD told us, while a former music teacher said the strict discipline had meant his lessons were taught in silence.

Athena is not the only academy trust that has enforced strict discipline.

There are those who argue that education built on tough discipline and high expectations can benefit pupils - and exam results at Athena-run schools have improved.

About 20% of the school day in England is lost to bad behaviour, the government says.

The benefits of a "high level of strictness" is that students understand what is expected of them, says the government advisor on behaviour in schools in England, Tom Bennett.

Commenting generally, rather than on individual academies, he told us that pupils soon realise they have to get into the habit of meeting expectations.

However, there is growing concern that punitive disciplinary practices at some schools in England are damaging children.

Athena's secondary schools are attended by about 6,500 children. In the past three years, more than 500 children have left to be educated at home, according to Cornwall and Devon county councils.

Amelia is one of them.

While at Camborne, Amelia would often come home with the bottle of water she had left with in the morning still full.

When Kayley asked Amelia why, she says her daughter would reply that she had not drunk anything all day, "so I wouldn't need to go to the toilet".

Camborne has strict rules around toilet visits during lessons.

Pupils were not allowed to go to the toilet in the first or last 15 minutes of a lesson, and were only allowed to go in the middle of a lesson at the teacher's discretion, pupils and former teachers told us.

On school days, Amelia would only drink after school and in the evening. Kayley believes her daughter's fear of breaking the rules ended up making her ill.

"She's now on antibiotics, she's had water infections, she has got scarring on her kidneys because of this," Kayley says.

Amelia says her time at Camborne "makes me feel ill, even thinking of it".

Athena told Panorama that staff work hard to "support children to remain in education" and "support access to toilets during lessons" through professional staff judgement.

Academies are independent, state-funded schools, that receive their funding directly from central government, rather than through a local authority. They have independent control over their own admissions, curriculum and staff pay.

There are no academy trusts in Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland, but more than 80% of secondary schools in England are now run by them.

Multi-academy trusts like Athena oversee a network of schools. Athena's reports from the regulator, Ofsted, have mostly been positive.

Brian Maywood used to be the head of Launceston College in north Cornwall and was an English teacher there when Athena took over.

Initially he welcomed the trust's highly disciplined approach, and was pleased the school was "moving into a new way of learning".

But his opinion quickly shifted, he says, once he witnessed how the children were treated, calling it a "dictatorship".

The way students were spoken to at times "made me really, really uncomfortable", he adds.

He left the school last summer because of these reasons, he says.

It was the same for the former head of art, Estelle Pears.

"There is discipline and then there is being oppressed," she says. "It sounds dramatic, but that's what it became.

"If you're frightened of moving a pencil on a desk because you will get a sanction, that's beyond discipline."

Former Athena teachers who spoke to Panorama said they were forced to uphold the strict rules by the trust and that some made little sense.

Ieuan Horgan says his music lessons had to be taught in silence.

"At the start of the lesson, I would go through how to play the musical notation, and then the lesson would just be silent focus on trying to learn this musical notation," he says.

"They pushed for 100% distraction and disruption-free lessons - and 100% silent focus - in a music lesson."

Pupils have told Panorama they could be punished for minor offences and Bethany, who has just finished her GCSEs at Camborne, describes the strict and regimented approach as "demoralising" and "like you're being talked to like you were a primary school kid".

Athena schools have a two-strike policy: a warning for one mistake, sent out of the class for the second. Students then go to what is called "reflection" - a room where they work in silence from workbooks.

At Launceston College there were about 1,000 cases a month of pupils being sent to "reflection" rooms between September 2025 and March 2026, according to figures released by the trust.

Athena says reflection rooms are "supervised environments" where "students continue their learning independently".

It says it does not have a rigid two strikes policy and the "vast majority of students spend little or no time in these spaces". Students are not normally punished for isolated minor issues, it adds.

Some parents say children with special educational needs and disabilities are disproportionately affected by Athena's strict policies.

April, whose son Jack has special educational needs and has just finished his GCSEs at Ilfracombe Academy, says he was sent to reflection countless times.

He could not cope with the regimented environment, she says.

"Just to look out the window to refocus, that's not harming any of the other children or their education within the room - but that's enough to be sent out, because that's him not focusing on the teacher."

Jack was also suspended - sent home from school - dozens of times. He is far from alone.

The suspension rate at Ilfracombe Academy was almost five times higher than the average in England, according to government figures for 2023 to 2025. At Camborne, it was about five times higher than the average and three times higher at Launceston, according to the same figures.

Athena says suspensions are reserved for "serious or repeated breaches of behaviour expectations" and that rates have fallen significantly in the past year.

April and Jack's concerns were echoed at our town-hall events. More than half of the dozens of parents and pupils who turned up were concerned about the impact on students with special educational needs.

Finn, a student at Camborne with ADHD, says it was a difficult environment for neurodiverse pupils. "You're constantly scared that you're going to do something wrong," he says.

Faye, whose son has special educational needs and attends Pool Academy, says he had spent 96 hours in reflection the past school year. "Day in, day out, he feels like he's failing," she says.

And Zara says her autistic daughter Hannah, who has hearing difficulties and attends Ilfracombe Academy, was repeatedly removed from class because her needs were not recognised.

"Behaviour is just put down to persistent defiance and bad behaviour, and they're punished for it," she says. "It's never recognised as being linked to their disabilities."

Athena told us that children with special educational needs are "not routinely sanctioned for behaviours associated with their needs".

A lot of the anger we heard in Devon and Cornwall is, we were told, down to the lack of accountability.

Academy trusts do not have any supervision from local councils, meaning only central government can intervene.

One of the biggest weaknesses of the trust system is that it complicates the complaints process, says education journalist Laura McInerney, who co-founded Teacher Tapp, an app designed to track educators' wellbeing, classroom practices, and opinions on education policy.

If parents are not satisfied with a specific school's response, she says, they have to contact the trust, which could be miles way, and which "you may or may not hear from in anything other than a letter".

The government says parents can take complaints about academy trusts to the Department for Education.

Across England, there is growing concern about punitive disciplinary practices in schools.

The BBC's File on 4 Investigates recently found that a school in Wakefield, West Yorkshire, put a pupil in an isolation booth away from the classroom for more than half an academic year.

A safeguarding review last year also found an east London school's zero-tolerance policy involved pupils being routinely humiliated by shouting and prioritised control above all else, leaving some children with lasting psychological harm.

A team at law firm Leigh Day is now investigating potential legal claims on behalf of 50 families who believe their children may have been subjected to excessive or inappropriate disciplinary measures while at school.

However, there are many who argue that education built on tough discipline and high expectations can benefit pupils.

The government's advisor on behaviour, Tom Bennett, told us that discipline is vital, including for children with special educational needs.

"If you've got, for example, ADHD or an anxiety disorder, what you need more than anybody else is a calm, safe, dignified environment. Otherwise, you'll be massively distracted by the environment round about you," Bennett says.

In Devon and Cornwall, parents appear to have won in their campaign against Athena.

In May, the head of the trust, who implemented the tough discipline, resigned.

Last month, the trust announced it was planning to disband.

In a statement, Athena said it had "listened carefully" and recognised the "clear need for change". It said it would work with the Department for Education to "identify alternative trusts" to which the schools could transfer.

Until then, Athena will keep running the schools.

The Department for Education told Panorama the allegations about Athena are "serious and concerning" and that it is "taking robust action to make sure the trust improves" ahead of the schools transferring.

The trust is now "subject to enhanced monitoring" to make sure its "approach to pupil behaviour is reasonable and proportionate", it says.

Bethany says the school has caused "incredible harm".

"They need to change the way that they're thinking they can teach students as a one-size-fits-all."

title: Why keeping youth discontent in check remains Indian PM Modi's biggest challenge
summary: India has the biggest youth population in the world but few are able to find good jobs despite rising education levels.
full_text:
Dharmendra Pradhan was forced to resign as India's education minister last month after angry Gen-Z protesters took to the streets over repeated entrance exam paper leaks.

His departure has allowed Prime Minister Narendra Modi to tide over an immediate crisis, but keeping youth discontent in check may well remain a long-term challenge for his government.

While Modi quickly announced fast-track courts , externalto try those accused in the leaks and appointed tech billionaire Nandan Nilekani to lead a government effort to reform the examination system, a more concerted effort may be needed to quell the anxieties of the young, who say they are losing patience with a system that's unable to offer them better livelihood opportunities or education that leads to productive employment.

"The labour market has become brutal in the last 10 years. Non-farm jobs have not been growing and real wages have stagnated," Santosh Mehrotra, a veteran economist and author of a new book India Out of Work: Rethinking India's Growth Story, told the BBC.

"India has a simultaneous problem. The economy is structurally weak as a result of which demand for labour is not growing. And our education system is so poor, that it is unable to supply new labour that is employable."

So far, rapid GDP growth fuelled by heavy state expenditure on infrastructure has been the government's default defence against criticism about the uneven nature of India's economic growth trajectory.

But the upheaval of the last month may finally push them to confront the crisis in education and the challenge of youth unemployment, say experts.

The "unprecedented growth in India's welfare state", particularly direct cash transfers, is an indication, Mehrotra says, that at least privately the government has recognised the problem.

But the task of fixing it is enormous.

India has the world's largest youth population with over 360 million people between the ages of 15 and 29.

There's been great progress in education enrolment and the number of private colleges and vocational training institutes have gone up exponentially in the last two decades.

However, "the transition from education to employment remains a major challenge, particularly for graduates", according to the State of Working India 2026 report , externalfrom Azim Premji University.

Unemployment rates among the young are nearly four times higher than the non-youth and also much higher than global averages.

The problem is not new. Graduate unemployment has hovered around the 35-40% level for the last 25 years.

But it has been "magnified" in recent years owing to India's demographic surge - or a growing size of the population entering the workforce - and improved education outcomes.

In 1983, 4% of 20 to 29-year-olds were graduates, and 13% of them were unemployed. In 2023, 28% were graduates and among them 67% were not employed.

Quality of education remains a major challenge affecting employability while the expansion in the number of graduates has not been matched by commensurate growth in graduate employment.

"Between 2004-05 and 2023, while approximately five million graduates were added each year, only around 2.8 million found employment, and an even smaller share entered salaried employment, contributing to rising graduate unemployment and slowing earnings growth," the report finds.

Moreover, there is no evidence that aspiration is being rewarded. Barely 3.7% of graduates or post-graduates found white collar work and under 7% landed permanent salaried jobs, according to the report.

This isn't a problem with short-term fixes.

"Some jobs can definitely come from a quick revival of the small and medium sized industries (SMEs) which have been completely knocked out since "demonetisation" [when 86% of India's currency was taken out of circulation in four hours in what was a widely criticised policy move] and the uneven implementation of a goods and services tax," says Mehrotra.

However, India will need to think of a new industrial policy to focus on reviving overall manufacturing, he adds.

"Manufacturing's share of GDP has gone down from 17% in 2015 to 14% currently. And manufacturing employment fell for five years after 2015 and has only now climbed back up slightly above those levels."

Meanwhile, Mehrotra says, total employment in agriculture has actually risen by 80 million people after 2020, a sure sign of disguised unemployment. This is because workers in a fast industrialising economy typically move out of agriculture into services or manufacturing as seen across the world.

All of these challenges have been compounded by the fact that the business model of key job-creating industries like software - a mainstay of the Indian middle class dream for three decades - has been challenged by the advent of AI.

In a recent report, Wall Street Bank Goldman Sachs estimates that 8-12% of non-farm jobs in India are at the risk of being substituted by AI. And the effects of that are already showing.

IT hiring has risen in single digits in recent months, unstable contract work is rising, wages have remained stagnant for years and the knowledge-based jobs that Indian STEM graduates took for granted two decades ago are no longer around in big numbers, according to Neeti Sharma, CEO of Team Lease Digital, one of India's most prominent staffing agencies.

In fact a recent event, external of HCL Technologies, one of the country' biggest software companies, in Chennai was disrupted by hundreds of employees chanting "we want a hike" in unison, reflecting the frustrations of an industry that was once the golden ticket to a better life.

"Young graduates will have to rewire their brains to the new reality that white-collar knowledge jobs are going down. And education institutions will have to pivot to providing vocational skills rather than just knowledge-based learning. Because the hiring has also moved from degrees to actual skills," Sharma told the BBC.

That is short-hand for saying young Indians with even graduate degrees may have to contend with the reality of working as plumbers, electricians and mechanics and not necessarily expect to have cushy careers in air-conditioned offices.

This means, as Devina Mehra, a leading market investor, observed on X, external, we are talking of a generation that can no longer take for granted a lifestyle better than that of their parents.

To be plateauing in earnings at such an early stage of India's development, Mehra says, could be a "disaster" - one that the Modi government will have to work very hard to prevent.
