title: OPINION: America’s teacher shortage is worse than you think. But there’s a way to fix it
summary:
When I was an assistant principal in Chicago, I would post a job opening for a physics teacher and get 20 applications. A call for an English teacher might yield 150. That was the late 1990s. By the time I left the district, the same postings were lucky to bring in one or two qualified […]

The post OPINION: America’s teacher shortage is worse than you think. But there’s a way to fix it appeared first on The Hechinger Report.
full_text:
When I was an assistant principal in Chicago, I would post a job opening for a physics teacher and get 20 applications. A call for an English teacher might yield 150.

That was the late 1990s. By the time I left the district, the same postings were lucky to bring in one or two qualified candidates.

Principals were calling the central office and saying, “Send me whoever you have.”

What happened to all the candidates? That question has never been fully answered in the national conversation about teacher shortages, in part because too much of that conversation has been devoted to arguing over whether a shortage exists at all. It does. And the cost of pretending otherwise falls on students who can least afford it.

The standard rebuttal to teacher shortage claims is a national one: Aggregate supply, measured against aggregate demand, looks roughly balanced. Recent headlines about teacher layoffs may seem to bolster that argument. But most of those layoffs are driven by enrollment declines, expiring pandemic relief funds or district budget cuts, not by a sudden surplus of qualified teachers.

Related: A lot goes on in classrooms from kindergarten to high school. Keep up with our free weekly newsletter on K-12 education.

A district may eliminate some positions because it has fewer dollars to spend, while still struggling to hire special education teachers, bilingual educators or high school physics teachers. Budget reductions change how many positions a district can afford; they don’t solve the longstanding challenge of finding qualified teachers for the schools, grade levels and subject areas where they’re still desperately needed.

Data backs this up. An estimated 425,000 teaching positions are either vacant or filled by underqualified staff — roughly one in eight of all teaching positions nationally.

And these vacancies aren’t distributed evenly across subjects and school districts. Forty-eight states report significant teacher shortages in special education, where vacancies are twice as common as in other specialties. In Illinois, vacancies in the wealthiest districts dropped 31 percent since 2023, an analysis by the Center for Tax and Budget Accountability found, while in the poorest districts they declined just 5 percent. In Chicago Public Schools, specifically, they actually rose 21 percent, though efforts are underway to fix the pipeline.

When a district can’t fill a position, it faces a choice: Leave the classroom empty or lower the bar. Most simply lower the bar, and in turn, feed the problem. Teachers with emergency permits or provisional licenses and individuals with no teaching background are placed in front of students who need the most support. Those teachers are also far more likely to leave, the Learning Policy Institute reports, creating a cycle of instability that is hardest on the schools already struggling to attract talent.

Nor is this just about teachers retiring. Ninety percent of teacher demand is driven by attrition, and about two-thirds of teachers leave for reasons other than retirement. Teachers are leaving because of deteriorating working conditions, declining professional prestige and the growing challenges of the job.

I understand why. During my first month in the role, I cried every day. Teaching, especially at the beginning, can be profoundly isolating. Without mentors and peers who understand the struggle, many new teachers leave before they have a chance to succeed.

Related: Federal policies risk worsening an already dire rural teacher shortage

The good news: A handful of districts and states are proving there’s a better way. Their teacher recruitment and preparation programs share a few things in common.

First, they recruit deliberately. They target young people who want to make a social impact, and who grew up in the very communities they hope to serve. In Hatch, New Mexico — a state where 36 percent of all teacher vacancies are in special education — Maria Gomez, a Hatch Valley High School graduate, returned to her alma mater and made it her mission to send other local students into the profession.

The students she mentored are now returning as teachers themselves, recruited not with broad messaging but with a specific pitch: You understand these kids, because you were one of them. This is a plus: Research shows that students fare better academically when taught by someone who shares their background, and teachers with roots in a community are more likely to stay.

They get candidates into classrooms early. No aspiring teacher should discover teaching isn’t for them during their student teaching semester in their senior year of college. Effective programs put future educators in real classrooms early and often. In 2018, Michigan began requiring teacher candidates to have at least 600 hours of clinical experience as part of the state’s approved educator preparation programs. This requirement ensures that teachers build skills and gain classroom exposure throughout their training, not just at the end. Michigan is now certifying more teachers than at any time in the past decade, a step toward filling vacancies.

They build community. It helps to build cohorts of people going through the same experience at the same time and to pair aspiring teachers with mentors whose job is to help them grow. Josh Payne, an instructional coach in Aurora, Illinois, knows this from experience. Josh participated in a teacher preparation program that placed him in a cohort of new teachers upon graduation and paired him with mentors. In a recent conversation, Payne shared that the program kept him from leaving and inspired him to become a mentor himself. Today, he said, his school district has six teachers from the same program that prepared him.

None of this is magic. But it requires treating teaching as a profession worth entering, not a gap to fill with whoever is available. The next time a principal calls the central office asking for whoever is available, there should be an answer:

“Here are 20 qualified candidates.”

The pipeline exists and can be built. Now leaders must act.

Alan Mather is the president of Golden Apple Foundation, a nonprofit dedicated to inspiring, developing and recognizing excellence in teaching and leading in education.

title: Pace of college closings picks up, with more projected
summary:

More than 440 of the nation’s private, nonprofit four-year colleges and universities are now at risk, based on enrollment trends, debt […]

The post Pace of college closings picks up, with more projected appeared first on The Hechinger Report.
full_text:
Pssst — wanna buy a college campus?

There’s a sudden market in abandoned campuses, an outgrowth of the accelerating rate of colleges closing in the face of falling enrollment, rising debt and other problems.

More than 440 of the nation’s private, nonprofit four-year colleges and universities are now at risk, based on enrollment trends, debt and other measures, according to projections by Huron Consulting Group. That’s a quarter of the total.

Among the most endangered: small, rural and religiously affiliated institutions.

And how to dispose of the real estate is among the least of the challenges facing shuttering campuses and the students they serve.

Fewer than half of students at colleges that close continue their educations, according to a study by the State Higher Education Executive Officers Association. Of those who do, only half go on to earn degrees. Some 670,000 students are enrolled at those colleges and universities that the Huron analysis found to be in trouble.

Related: Interested in innovations in higher education? Subscribe to our free biweekly higher education newsletter.

There are several reasons colleges are closing.

A decline in the birthrate that began around the Great Recession means there will be 15 percent fewer 18-year-olds per year through 2039 than there are now. That’s on top of a drop in the number of students on campus that began in 2011; college and university enrollment is already down by about 2 million since that time.

Among that falling number of high school graduates, the proportion going straight to college has also dropped, from a peak of 70 percent to just under 63 percent in 2024, the most recent year for which the figure is available from the Bureau of Labor Statistics.

International students, who universities and colleges recruited to help fill that gap, have stopped coming, too, in the face of tightened visa rules and higher costs. That is forcing cuts to programs, services and staffing for domestic students. And new limits on federal loans for graduate and professional school could reduce demand for programs that provide universities with badly needed revenue.

While times may be tough for colleges, there’s good news for prospective students. As demand falls, acceptance rates are going up; the median acceptance rate to bachelor’s degree-granting colleges and universities rose by at least 7.6 percentage points from 2012 to 2022.

Related: More than a quarter of private colleges are at risk of closing, new projection shows

Some institutions are admitting students who haven’t even applied, waiving application fees and offering financial aid to prospects just for visiting.

Still, the accomplishment of getting into college — and doing it at a discount — can be hollow if the college doesn’t stay in operation long enough to get students to graduation. So lawmakers are responding to the industry’s decline by adding or proposing new consumer protections.

In Massachusetts, for example, where 27 colleges have shut down or announced they will shut down since 2014, a state law now requires private colleges and universities to provide financial reports to anyone who wants to see them. Those schools at imminent likelihood of closing are named publicly.

Related: Threats of more closings have colleges and students worrying about how to save themselves

Twenty-two states make private higher education institutions pay into “tuition recovery” funds for students to be compensated if they close. There’s a proposal to add a similar provision at the federal level, where policymakers are also promising to streamline the process by which troubled colleges can be merged with healthier competitors instead of going out of business.

If that doesn’t work, one company has a backup plan to memorialize closed colleges, at least for the nostalgia value: by creating virtual tours of campuses that close.

The first such virtual-reality tour will be of Trinity Christian College, in Palos Heights, Illinois, which closed in May.

“Instead of being wiped off the map, this is a way to honor the legacy” of defunct colleges, said Shalom Nwaokolo, who co-runs the company. That way, added his wife and business partner, Ashley, “people can have some history to go back to.”

title: Are Loan Limits Driving Down College Costs?
summary:
Are Loan Limits Driving Down College Costs?
jessica.blake@… Mon, 08/03/2026 - 03:00 AM

The Education Department and some policy experts say yes. But others aren’t so sure.

Byline(s)
Jessica Blake
full_text:
When Republicans set new loan limits for graduate students last summer, they made it clear their intent was to drive down college costs and address the mounting student debt crisis. Now, as those limits take effect ahead of a new academic year, some are saying that goal is already coming to fruition.

A new blog from the American Enterprise Institute, a right-leaning think tank, says that graduate programs are “cutting tuition,” citing 10 programs across the country—seven of which are providing scholarships rather than directly reducing tuition. In many cases, the colleges making these changes pointed to the Republican loan limits, added Preston Cooper, a senior fellow at AEI and author of the blog.

For example, Emory University announced in November that it would offer a $25,000 tuition scholarship to any student who applied for its online Doctor of Public Health, accelerated Master of Public Health, or hybrid Master of Health Administration programs by January.

“In light of recent changes to graduate student loan programs, these funds will help students invest in their education while minimizing the burden of significant debt,” said Kara Robinson, Emory’s senior associate dean of enrollment management and student affairs, in the announcement.

But not all colleges AEI cited explicitly tied the decision to the new loan limits. Still, “if you kind of read between the lines a little bit, that is probably something that is on their minds,” Cooper said.

The Education Department has shared similar examples, and, in most cases, the financial adjustment applies to specific degree programs, rather than to an entire college or university. Some of the changes are based on income level or only apply to in-state students or those registered as graduate assistants.

Still, Cooper argues “this is early signs that the loan limits seem to be working.”

House Republicans on the education committee are also touting AEI’s blog, saying in a news release that it “demonstrates schools are already responding by lowering prices—a positive sign that [the education provisions of the One Big Beautiful Bill] are beginning to restore sanity in college pricing resulting in better value for students and taxpayers.”

But not everyone is on the same page. Some more left-leaning policy experts say the examples Cooper lists are just a fraction of graduate programs overall, so it’s too soon to tell whether the loan limits are working, especially as litigation challenging the new rule continues and many institutions wait to see how the policy plays out. Critics also note that the majority of the listed examples don’t directly lower a program’s sticker price; instead, they guarantee scholarships to cover the difference between the new federal loan limits and existing tuition rates.

“Even if the programs that have been identified as lowering their prices for some set of their students were [actually lowering cost for] entire institutions, it would still be a fraction of the colleges in the country. So it’s way too early to argue that costs have gone down, and it’s pretty bold to assume that they will,” said Clare McCann, managing director of the Postsecondary Education and Economics Research (PEER) Center at American University. “There will be changes to how colleges price, but it is not remotely clear at this point that that will be universally or even widely in the interests of many borrowers.”

A December study from PEER and the Federal Reserve Bank of Philadelphia’s Consumer Finance Institute shows that about 28 percent of graduate borrowers take out loans above the new federal limits; on average, they’d need to find about $21,700 to fill the gap. And, of those borrowers, nearly four in 10 (38 percent) have either poor credit scores or have no credit score at all, which could make it difficult, or even impossible, to obtain private loans.

Still, if the net cost drops for certain students in certain programs, McCann argues it doesn’t indicate that college costs are collectively heading down. Providing discounts for some students, rather than changing the sticker price, allows colleges to help new students adapt to the loan limits while continuing to charge existing students full price, McCann noted. It’s also far easier to retract a scholarship than raise prices should loan limit regulations change, she said.

But McCann also isn’t opposed to the scholarships for now. She doesn’t think the current loan limits are the best way to lower college cost and hopes to eventually see more nuanced loan policies based on how students fare in the programs.

“One important component of thinking about college costs is understanding whether the school is investing enough in the instruction of the program to provide a sufficient quality education. So you wouldn’t want to simply drive down costs without thinking about the trade-offs that are being made,” she explained. By creating scholarships, colleges are “trying to lower the price at least some students will pay [without risking loss of quality], but it’s not necessarily indicative that the cost itself has changed.”

Ben Cecil, deputy director of higher education policy at Third Way, a left-of-center think tank that often advocates for students, fell somewhere in between Cooper and McCann. In his view, scholarships change the net cost and allow students to pay less—so to some degree that is an example of costs coming down. But on the institutional side, does that mean tuition is really being lowered? Or are they just moving money around?

“The answer is far more complicated there,” Cecil said.

Providing scholarships also helps accomplish one of Cecil’s primary goals beyond just lowering college cost: ensuring a more equal distribution of investment risk. As you lower college costs, Cecil said, it’s also important to ask how institutions, and sometimes private lenders, can take on more responsibility. That way, it’s not just students and taxpayers carrying all of the burden, if the investment doesn’t pay off.

“What you’re seeing in [Cooper’s blog], is a lot of schools coming to the table to try to help answer that question proactively,” he explained.

Cooper acknowledged some institutions are waiting before they “pull the trigger.” But he believes the evidence suggests that universities are lowering tuition and the list of colleges doing so should only expand.

“I’m really glad that a lot of these schools are cutting tuition,” he said. “It’s going to make a real difference in the lives of students who have to spend less of their own money and take on less debt to pursue a graduate degree at one of these institutions.”

title: Inheriting the Disenchanted
summary:
Inheriting the Disenchanted
sara.custer@in… Mon, 08/03/2026 - 03:00 AM

Persistence matters.

Byline(s)
Matt Reed
full_text:
Christine Nowik recently published a piece that has been scratching at my brain for the last several days. It’s about what she calls employee disenchantment, which she usefully distinguishes from burnout. Burnout, in her telling, comes from too much work; disenchantment comes from losing faith that their best efforts matter. A disenchanted employee may be perfectly functional in the obvious, measurable ways, but won’t go above and beyond to offer risky insights or extra effort because they’ve seen those efforts either backfire or come to nothing too many times. They withdraw. Over time, the organization loses the insights it could have gained if the employee had felt like there was some point in trying.

She’s on to something; the piece is well worth reading in its entirety. (The gardening metaphor works particularly well.) And I’d be lying if I said I had never felt that way at various points in my career. But I’ll build on her insight by coming from a different angle.

Several times in my career, I’ve moved to a new institution. When you arrive as a dean or a VP at a new institution, you “inherit” the people who are already there. Some are relatively new, but many will have been there for some time. It feels like joining a show already in progress; you see people responding to history you don’t have access to, and you have to piece together narratives in real time. Part of the “drinking from a fire hose” cliché that new managers often say—I’ve said it myself—is precisely that: You’re trying to read the unwritten rules even while getting things done. It takes time and a lot of mental energy.

That doesn’t mean that hiring from the outside is always bad. Hires from the outside can bring different experiences and fresh eyes. It just means that some amount of learning curve is to be expected.

I once arrived at an institution just a few months after a major reduction in force (RIF). It was the first major layoff in its history, and the culture was reeling. Many terrific people were feeling betrayed or worse, and the background level of trust was suffering. In some ways, it felt like a sort of organizational PTSD. Coming in immediately after that was more difficult than I had realized at the time. An entire cohort had been disenchanted at the same time. Getting traction for good ideas was much harder than it should have been, because nobody wanted to be accused of being complicit with The Administration, even if the new guy had nothing to do with the RIF and the idea made sense.

Sometimes the issues are more idiosyncratic. At a couple of places, I’ve inherited people who—seemingly for reasons of their own—had crossed over to a kind of toxic cynicism bordering on nihilism. They would assume bad faith almost as a reflex and would immediately ascribe the worst possible motives to nearly anything. Coming in as a new person, it was jarring; I was guilty until proven innocent, and any proof was suspect. Sometimes they would eventually sense that the culture had moved on without them, and they’d leave; others just dug in for the long haul, spewing bile whenever approached. At a certain point, I had to learn to work around them if I wanted to get anything done. I’d reflect on the Dr. Seuss story about the North-Going Zax and the South-Going Zax, sigh, and get back to work.

Re-enchanting the disenchanted is a serious challenge. (Nowik’s “losing the clubhouse” borders on suggesting that it simply can’t be done.) I have to believe it can be done, and I’ve actually seen it happen to a limited degree. But it’s hard, and victories tend to be partial at best. I’ve said for years that the job of administration is to establish the background conditions in which people can do their best work. That happens within the limits of public funding, local demographics, and all manner of variables, of course, but over time, people can usually sense direction.& They can tell when someone is motivated by ego or careerism, and when they’re motivated by a desire to do the right thing. Sticking to the latter can be difficult, especially in the early stages when the toxic ones are testing you, but it matters.

My thanks to Nowik for labeling something real. It’s a helpful reminder that what seem like immutable character traits are often learned, and, I have to hope, can be unlearned. The task of leadership is to foster the environment in which that’s possible.

title: What Parents Prioritize in the College Search
summary:
What Parents Prioritize in the College Search
Johanna Alonso Mon, 08/03/2026 - 03:00 AM
Byline(s)
Johanna Alonso
full_text:
Parents are increasingly concerned about their students’ job prospects after college, according to a new report from the enrollment management firm EAB about parents and the college search process. The report draws on a survey of 2,515 parents conducted in spring 2026.

Twenty-nine percent of respondents cited post-graduation job prospects as one of their top five concerns when evaluating where their child will attend college, an 81 percent increase from the last time the survey was conducted, in 2024. But the overall price of college remains the most common concern, with 64 percent selecting it as one of their top worries, followed by school fit (50 percent), financial aid (41 percent) and mental wellbeing (40 percent).

Parents at all stages of the college search process said they were most interested in receiving information about cost of attendance and financial aid from the colleges and universities their student is considering. Broadly, the majority of parents (71 percent) said they wanted institutions to communicate with them directly. And while over half of parents said the amount of contact they received from institutions was “just right,” 69 percent said they didn’t feel the information was “very” or “extremely” useful.

Ninety-three percent of parents surveyed said they were “moderately” or “extremely” involved in the college search process. But they said they were more likely to participate in financial decisions—like how much to spend on college or take out in loans—than in which institutions their student should apply to.

title: House Ethics panel recommends censure for Chuck Edwards after harassment allegations
summary: After a months-long investigation, the ethics committee recommended censure for Edwards because of "persistent unprofessional and inappropriate conduct towards two young female staffers."
full_text:
The House Ethics Committee is recommending that Rep. Chuck Edwards be censured because of "persistent unprofessional and inappropriate conduct towards two young female staffers."

The committee has been investigating the North Carolina Republican for months and published its 20-page report on Monday.

The bipartisan committee said it did not find evidence that the congressman propositioned his staffers or engaged in sexual activity with them.

The report states that in his interview with the committee, Edwards asserted he understood "sexual harassment."

"[He] seemed to believe that by avoiding inappropriate physical touch, explicitly sexual comments, and occasionally telling staffers that they were free to put up boundaries with him, he had immunized himself from such a charge," the report reads. "That is not the case."

The panel investigated allegations that Edwards, who took office in 2023, may have created a hostile work environment and engaged in sexual harassment.

In a statement, a spokesman for Edwards' reelection campaign took issue with the panel's report, alleging committee staff "has taken it upon themselves to write their own rules based upon an interpretation that is inconsistent with the written rule of law or House rules."

"Representative Edwards looks forward to having his name cleared and will work to ensure that the full light of day is brought on this process and that every member of Congress and the public can see the attempt to harm the Congressman who has brought no harm to others," said spokesman Paul Shumaker.

In a separate rebuttal to the committee's report, lawyers for the congressman said the panel had failed to demonstrate that the staffers expressed their discomfort to Edwards.

"Representative Edwards has been denied the opportunity to challenge the factual allegations guaranteed to him under House rules," they wrote. They also said the congressman "sincerely regrets that his behavior created discomfort" for either of the two staffers.

The investigation details his interactions with two young female staffers, including showering them with "lavish and recurrent gifts," including jewelry totaling over $1,000, designer purses, guns, shoes, flowers, a laptop and cell phone, KitchenAid mixer, vacations and one-on-one-dinners.

The report also found that the congressman made comments regarding these staffers' appearances, invited them to intimate dinners and vacations, and sent them notes "regarding his effusive affection."

The report said both women attempted to communicate their discomfort with their boss's behavior, and that ultimately, a senior staffer spoke to Edwards on their behalf.

That staffer testified that Edwards, 65, said she "didn't understand the unique relationship" he had with them.

Edwards cooperated with the committee's investigation, which included 16 witness interviews, including the congressman himself, and over 1,500 pages of evidence.

The committee voted to issue this report on July 22.

The House is currently on recess, so the censure itself would not take place until at least September. A censure is the strongest punishment the panel can recommend short of expulsion. It is tantamount to a public shaming on the House floor.

title: A $104 billion question: are we preparing students for jobs that no longer exist?
summary:
Australia's international education sector contributes more than AU$53 billion to the economy each year, making it one of the nation's most valuable exports. Yet an even larger figure should be demanding our attention, says Pearson's Taha Haidermota.

The post A $104 billion question: are we preparing students for jobs that no longer exist? appeared first on The PIE News.
full_text:
According to recent Pearson modelling, inefficient transitions between education, work and reskilling cost the Australian economy an estimated AUS$104 billion annually.

While much of that cost is linked to workforce disruption and automation, the figure points to the broader challenge that moving people successfully from learning into meaningful work is becoming increasingly difficult.

At a time when artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming industries, reshaping roles and changing the skills employers value, that challenge is only becoming more urgent.

For higher education, this raises a fundamental question: are we preparing students for jobs that no longer exist?

For decades, universities have operated on a clear proposition. Students invest in education to gain knowledge, develop skills and improve their career prospects. Institutions support them through that journey and help prepare them for the workforce.

That promise still matters. But the nature of work itself is changing.

Increasingly, success depends not only on what someone knows at graduation, but on their ability to continue learning, adapt and apply new skills throughout their career. Graduates will need practical AI capability, resilience and employer-recognised skills to navigate a rapidly evolving workforce.

This was a recurring theme throughout discussions at The PIE Live Asia Pacific. While conversations spanned student recruitment, market diversification, policy settings and institutional strategy, many returned to a central question: how can international education continue to deliver value in a changing world?

Across discussions on Australia’s position in the global education market, skills recognition and employment pathways, there was a shared recognition that students are placing greater focus on the return on their educational investment.

They are not simply asking where a qualification might take them. They are increasingly considering the learner journey beyond graduation and whether their education will prepare them for meaningful work, future opportunities and long-term career success.

Will this qualification help me find meaningful work?

Future-ready graduates will need to understand when to use AI, when to challenge it, when to explain its limitations and when to apply human judgement

Will my skills still be relevant when I graduate?

Will employers recognise the capabilities I have developed?

And perhaps most importantly, will I be able to adapt when my industry changes?

Graduate employment rates remain important, but they tell only part of the story. They measure whether someone secured a role after university. They tell us far less about whether that person is equipped to navigate a career that may involve multiple transitions, new technologies and entirely different ways of working.

In many ways, our traditional understanding of employability is rooted in a labour market that no longer exists.

The concept of being “job ready” implies a relatively stable destination. Students acquire knowledge and skills, enter the workforce and apply what they have learned.

However, AI is accelerating change across almost every profession, and the challenge is preparing students to navigate occupations that will continue evolving long after graduation.

This requires a broader definition of workforce readiness, one that focuses not only on preparing people for their first role, but equipping them to continually build new capabilities as industries evolve.

That means embedding a mindset of “learning to learn” across education and training, creating more flexible, modern skilling pathways through apprenticeships, industry partnerships and tailored work-based learning opportunities, and better recognising reputable global qualifications and skills so talented people can contribute fully from day one.

Future-ready graduates will need to understand when to use AI, when to challenge it, when to explain its limitations and when to apply human judgement. In an AI-enabled economy, competitive advantage will increasingly come from combining technological capability with uniquely human skills.

Communication. Critical thinking. Adaptability. Collaboration. Ethical decision-making.

This is where international education has a significant opportunity.

The international student experience often develops many of the capabilities the future workforce requires. Students navigating unfamiliar systems, adapting to new environments and communicating across cultures build resilience, problem-solving skills and the ability to operate in complex situations.

These are not simply by-products of studying abroad. Increasingly, they are employability outcomes.

The challenge is ensuring students can recognise, articulate and demonstrate these capabilities in ways employers understand.

Universities can play a critical role by embedding employability more deeply throughout the student experience. Work-integrated learning, industry projects, authentic assessments and microcredentials can help students connect education with real-world application, while creating opportunities to practise the skills required in modern workplaces.

The AUS$104bn question is not simply about economics. It is about whether our education systems are enabling people to succeed across the entire learner journey, from exploring education pathways and developing skills, to entering the workforce, progressing through their careers and adapting to a lifetime of change.

Because in an AI economy, employability is no longer a destination reached at graduation. It is the ability to keep adapting throughout a lifetime of change.

title: US: Trump administration considers $100,000 OPT fee
summary:
The Trump administration is reportedly weighing a plan to fix a $100,000 fee onto America’s post-graduation employment program for international students known as Optional Practical Training (OPT).

The post US: Trump administration considers $100,000 OPT fee appeared first on The PIE News.
full_text:
If enacted, the proposal would effectively bar thousands of international students from participating in OPT, having a potentially devastating impact on inbound international mobility to US universities.

Exclusively broken yesterday by the Washington Post, news of the plans came through a person familiar with the matter speaking under anonymity.

The plans are purportedly still under discussion, and a spokesperson for the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) said “no policies should be considered final until formally announced”, but did not deny it was under consideration.

“Our immigration system is being reformed to serve American citizens, American workers, and American families and to preserve our national identity – not to rapidly import foreigners who take American jobs, commit crimes, steal our intellectual property and engage in corporate espionage, and erode our cultural and social fabric,” they told The PIE News.

In its current form, OPT offers international students an opportunity to work in the US for 12 months. Those taking STEM OPT have the option to extend their work period by a further two years.

International students remain on their F-1 visa for the duration of the program, though following the administration’s final rule ending duration of status, from September they will be required to file for an extension of stay with DHS.

The program has been central to America’s appeal as the world’s largest host country of international students, with nearly 295,000 total OPT participants in 2024/25 according to the latest data from IIE.

The workstream’s growing popularity has been the driver of rising international student levels in recent years, with OPT participants counted in F-1 student totals.

In 2024/25, OPT saw a continued increase of 21% – just below the previous year’s growth rate and largely driven by Indian students who made up just under half (49%) of all OPT participants.

The university sector has long been anticipating a change to the post-graduation work program, with repeated calls from within government for its abolition, with the head of ICE recently branding the program a “magnet for fraud”.

It is understood that DHS is still planning a broad overhaul of OPT, with new regulations expected this fall.

Notably, if the rumoured $100,000 fee is enacted, it remains unclear whether the charge would be burdened by international students themselves or prospective universities and employers.

At DHS we are always having conversations about how to use all tools in our arsenal to protect the integrity of our legal immigration system

DHS

Last year, Trump’s shock announcement of a $100,000 fee on H-1B skilled worker visas was met with fierce criticism from US universities and prospective employers particularly in Silicon Valley.

It was later clarified that international students would be exempted from the charge, and last week a federal appeals court blocked the administration’s bid to start collecting the new $100,000 fee for H-1B visas.

If attached to OPT, the fee could drastically worsen the declining flow of international students to the US, with six in ten US colleges reporting a fall in international student applications following 18 months of policy turbulence and visa challenges during Trump’s second administration.

The workstream is commonly cited as one of the primary reasons for students choosing to study in the US, with over half of current postgraduate students indicating they wouldn’t have enrolled at an American university had OPT been rescinded, a recent NAFSA study found.

With more focus than ever on post-graduation work opportunities and questions about the ROI of a US degree, ill Colvin SVP global solutions at Shorelight described OPT as “the infrastructure for American success”.

I can’t imagine a world where we compete without OPT,” he said, speaking at a major industry conference earlier this year.

title: How Campus Network Infrastructure Defines Student Experience and Enrollment
summary:
The signals are undeniable: Modernized campus network infrastructure is now the central nervous system of a competitive higher education institution.
When the network stumbles, the institution feels it everywhere. That’s the shift we want more campus leaders to sit with. We used to think of digital infrastructure as more of a back-office concern. It isn’t anymore. The network, the security posture and the classroom technology now shape the student experience, influence enrollment and increasingly determine how competitive an institution can be over the long term.
Click the banner below for…
full_text:
Why Campus Network Infrastructure Is Mission-Critical for Higher Education

Proof that campus networks are mission-critical surfaced recently when the Canvas breach impacted students taking final exams. Across higher education, institutions suddenly found themselves scrambling. Students were locked out of coursework. And what looked like a software outage quickly became a campuswide disruption.

Schools ground to a halt. If the network isn’t robust and things aren’t working, everything from physical security access to lighting controls, heating and cooling, and plumbing systems is controlled via network capabilities.

How Higher Education IT Infrastructure Impacts Enrollment and Reputation

When a core system fails, schools don’t just experience an IT problem. Teaching stalls. Student services slow down. Confidence in the institution can take a hit, which can also impact reputation, institutional competitiveness and enrollment from prospective students.

If an interested student steps onto campus for a tour and faces broken guest Wi-Fi or lagging portals, that negative first impression undercuts a higher ed institution’s recruitment pipeline before students even apply — if they still want to.

LEARN MORE: An expert explains why higher ed classroom tech is an enrollment strategy.

The timing and quality of a school’s first meaningful interaction with a student heavily impacts downstream enrollment choices. Students who experience early, frictionless affinity-building are significantly more likely to follow through and enroll, according to education firm EAB’s Enrollment Insights report.

If you get a reputation for having outdated, antiquated equipment or a poor network experience, that information is going to travel quickly among students and potential students. It spreads through social media group chats and peer recommendations faster than a marketing campaign can counter.

A Phased Approach to Campus Infrastructure Refresh

And whether students are already enrolled or stepping on campus for their first day, the average student is coming to campus with seven or eight devices that all require internet connectivity. Strong, reliable internet connection is presumed to be a given. Students also expect that they won’t have to constantly join different networks when traveling between buildings or otherwise outside.

Each additional smartphone, tablet and student-owned laptop expands the attack surface and security vulnerabilities.

Moving to a zero-trust posture keeps the campus network and devices safe by requiring additional levels of authentication. While nothing is infallible, this means going an extra step further to make sure users are who they say they are. And if a password does get leaked, there’s a secondary layer of backup or security.

READ MORE: Being thoughtful about the “why” when it comes to network upgrades matters.

When it comes to maintaining modernization, one of the biggest mistakes that we see is applying upgrades to fix a very specific problem without tying it to a broader strategy for innovation. Patching the thing that broke rather than zooming out puts IT teams in a posture of having to constantly repair rather than moving forward.

Every dollar goes to the most recent emergency instead of linking fixes to broader, proactive strategies for innovation and planning. IT leaders who can develop a holistic plan that is tied to their institution’s overarching technology roadmap are best positioned to get out of that loop.

Refreshing is a never-ending process, especially with the way that technology cycles are structured. The goal isn’t to reach a finished state, because one doesn’t exist. Instead, a phased approach that includes a comprehensive understanding of the infrastructure and scheduled refreshes of the most pressing components supports the network — and the student experience by extension.

title: The three-way win for students, academics and employers
summary: The post The three-way win for students, academics and employers appeared first on Advance HE UK.
full_text:
NBSBright challenge is one of our business support initiatives and aligns with our personalisation and experiential learning strategy at Nottingham Business School, Nottingham Trent University. As part of this initiative, we have been working with final year students and HR/Business professionals from various organisations. The aim of this collaboration is to provide solutions to current business challenges through student-led projects supervised by experienced academics.

Over the years, we have worked with small, medium and large organisations from various sectors including not-for-profit, government and business organisations such as Next Retail, HM Revenue and Customs (HMRC), National Health Service (NHS), Accounting Plus Charity organisation and specialist HR organisations like Staffline among others. These organisations were enthusiastic about obtaining fresh, external perspectives and gaining potential solutions to some of their current challenges. Each organisation we worked with developed a detailed project brief outlining the challenges that should be addressed. We integrated these briefs into a final year, practice-based module as an assessed piece of work.

Working closely with students and supervising their groups as they tackle real business challenges has been a genuinely satisfying experience for us as academics. Client organisations have implemented students’ recommendations and acknowledged the value of the NBSBright Challenge in addressing real-world business challenges. Presenting these projects as summative assessment helped to secure strong student commitment and foster deeper engagement. These projects have been personally and professionally rewarding. In this blog, we aim to communicate some of the benefits of our collaborations with students and industry to spark motivations and encourage pedagogic innovations.

For students, the experience has created valuable opportunities to engage with senior HR/Business professionals from renowned organisations, working on real-life business issues, and building professional networks while strengthening their knowledge, skills, and employability. Through collaboration with academics, practitioners, and peers, students have been able to “move from legitimate peripheral participation into full participation” (Lave and Wenger, 1991, p. 37). As academics, we also benefit from this engagement, gaining first-hand insight into practitioner perspectives and the current business challenges from the experiences of business professionals. Practitioners who collaborate with academics and students claim that such engagements help challenge their predispositions and provide a renewed understanding of relevant theoretical perspectives and their application to business challenges.

We see this project as having real potential for wider impact, bringing together students, academics, and practitioners to co-create solutions to real business issues. The mix of students’ fresh perspectives, academic’ research insights, and practitioners’ expertise is a powerful and relatively rare combination, helping to bridge the practice-research gap (Kaufman, 2022). Moreover, innovative assessment strategies like the NBS Bright Challenge are timely as Artificial Intelligence is reshaping traditional approaches to assessments, and students’ learning and development. Projects of this nature have the potential to move beyond emphasis on authentic assessments in a professional context, as NBS Bright challenge project closely links a) contextual authenticity, (relevance to real life/disciplinary context); b) task authenticity (as it resembles professional practice); c) personal authenticity (project aligns with students’ career interests, values) (Zhang et al., 2025). As business schools and other institutions rethink assessment strategies to respond to AI, employability pressures, and questions of relevance, initiatives like the NBS Bright Challenge offer meaningful benefits for all stakeholders. Below, we outline some of the benefits we have experienced, with the aim of inspiring others to explore similar possibilities.

Impact of NBS bright Challenge

Leveraging academic research for practical business impact: Businesses gain evidence-based, research-informed solutions to current challenges with minimal cost implications, requiring only the time needed to develop the project brief and some engagement with student groups during the project period. This offers an opportunity to translate research into practice. Moreover, this project facilitates a positive collaborative model to address long-argued gaps between research and practice as it emphasises the relevance of both worlds, thereby challenging predispositions of both academics and practitioners.

Developing and building a talent pool through applied business projects: Experiential learning strategically positions students as an emerging talent pool, enabling organisations to engage early in the development of future capabilities. Through practice-based collaboration, businesses can actively shape, develop, and harness student talent, thereby strengthening organisational talent pipelines while ensuring graduates are work-ready, professionally agile, and aligned with evolving industry needs. In turn, students gain valuable insight into organisations in different sectors, helping them make informed career decisions based on real-life experiences of working with professionals. By working directly on current business challenges, students improve their ability to apply theoretical knowledge to practice in diverse contexts. This fosters problem-solving, creativity, and a deeper understanding of how academic concepts operate in the real world. Moreover, this initiative helps develop learners’ relevant skills, mindset, agency, and professionalism

Collaborative practice-informed teaching and learning: The project brings together students, academic staff and industry professionals, thereby promoting collaboration, knowledge exchange, and the development of future partnerships between higher education institutions and business practice, with evidence showing that industry-university partnerships enhance engagement, value creation, and long-term collaboration frameworks (Gutierrez et al., 2025). Academics gain exposure to contemporary industry issues, which enrich their teaching with practical relevance. Working alongside practitioners further strengthens the connection between research and practice (Kauffman, 2022) in curriculum development and review, resulting in good learning opportunities for all stakeholders.

Strengthening academic integrity through authentic assessment: It supports academic integrity by engaging students in real organisational projects that require primary analysis and applied problem solving, an approach which aligns with Zhan et al’s (2025) broader perspective of authentic assessment that covers contextual, task and personal authenticity. This assessment type reduces likelihood of plagiarism, academic misconduct, contract cheating, and inappropriate use of artificial intelligence tools, ensuring that student work reflects genuine learning and professional capability.

Building lifelong and life wide skills: The project reinforces students’ development as lifelong and lifewide learners by strengthening their transferable skills that remain valuable throughout their career. Students enhance their communication, teamwork, leadership, resilience, time management, and decision-making abilities. These essential skills extend beyond academic achievement, supporting students’ confidence, adaptability, and effectiveness in both business and personal life.

Future focus

Reflecting on our experience so far and the impact of these projects, we invite business schools around the world to explore how such initiatives can contribute meaningfully to both local and international businesses while strengthening student readiness, talent pipeline and relevance of academic research. Such initiatives will provide opportunities for business schools to ensure their learning, teaching, and research are at the heart of positive changes in the world of work. These projects also create valuable pathways for internships, work placements, contract research, engaged scholarships, and practice-based opportunities for academics. Moreover, there are potentials for co-teaching, assessment and feedback practices in collaboration with practitioners.

Looking ahead, our focus is firmly on deepening and scaling these collaborative partnerships. We recognise that many business schools in developing countries seem to have more gaps in how academic research, learning, teaching, and assessment practices address current business challenges. In response, we have started collaborating with such institutions, co-developing practices, sharing knowledge, and learning through mutual engagement. To strengthen our work, we aim to undertake further research that builds a richer, evidence-based understanding of relevant assessment practices. We thrive as a ‘business school for businesses’ as we continue to evolve through initiatives such as NBS Bright challenge, which exemplifies our commitment to embedding practice-focused, socially relevant, and industry-engaged learning at the core of our teaching, learning and research. We therefore encourage academics, business schools, and business organisations to critically reflect on their practices and explore ways of co-creating approaches that deliver sustained value for business schools, organisations, communities, and wider stakeholders. Through such partnerships, we see significant potential to address both business needs and broader societal challenges.

Duminda Rajasinghe, PhD is a senior lecturer in HRM and OB at Nottingham Trent University. Duminda’s research interest lies in coaching and adult learning. He works as an academic mentor and an executive coach at Nottingham Business school. He is a Senior Fellow of the AdvancedHE (SFHEA), Academic Member of CIPD and the Chair of external relations committee of University Forum of HRD.

Tolulope Fadipe, PhD, is Programme Lead for Business Management and Human Resources at Nottingham Business School. He leads a team dedicated to personalisation and experiential learning. His research explores organisational learning, knowledge management, and people wellbeing. He is a Senior Fellow of Advance HE and Academic Member of CIPD.

Kaufman, B.E. (2022). The academic-practitioner gap: Past time to bring in the practitioner perspective. Human Resource Management Review, 32(2), https://doi.org/10.1016/j.hrmr.2022.100895

title: Hyper-personalization in higher education recruitment: a new standard
summary: sk a prospective student what "personalized" outreach feels like and most will describe the opposite: a first-name mail merge that ignores everything else they've told you. This week, we look at what actually moves conversion.
full_text:
In a crowded higher education marketplace, standing out takes more than just large segments and blanket emails, we've all seen this.

Prospective students now expect tailored experiences from their first digital touchpoint all the way through to enrollment; it's just what they know.

Many of them are still receiving a "personalized" email from your university or college, with maybe their name at the top, or a generic brochure. Maybe a reference to a major they clicked on once, three months ago.

That's not personalization. That's a mail merge with better branding.

Hyper-personalization is a different standard entirely, and it's becoming the baseline, not the differentiator.

Students expect context-aware interactions because every other part of their digital life already delivers them

A prospective student who has a clear interest in a topic but receives content on another is going to tune out, not because the content is bad (everyone's working on this!), but because it's obviously not for them.

We know budgets are tight and there's more and more competition for the same shrinking pool of prospects.

And you can't just widen the funnel anymore, so what's to be done?

You've got to maximize the yield out of the inquiries already sitting in your higher ed CRM.

And while technology stopped being exclusive to well-funded flagships, CRM platforms, behavioral tracking, and AI-driven engagement tools are now within reach of mid-sized institutions with lean teams.

And the differentiator is orchestration, not the budget size.

Hyper-personalization isn't an experimental tactic anymore, it's become a strategic necessity for smart higher ed institutions trying to improve conversion, protect yield, and support students from day one of the recruitment journey.

Not sure about hyper-personalization? Let's see what actually looks like in higher ed recruitment, why it's become so important, and how institutions are putting it into practice.

What Is hyper-personalization?

Traditional personalization means dropping a first name into a mail-merge or grouping students into broad buckets like "STEM prospects" or "international applicants."

Hyper-personalization goes much further.

It uses real-time behavioral data, predictive modeling, and AI-driven engagement to adapt messaging to an individual's interests, context, and stage in the funnel.

So where before you would have asked which campaign a student should get next, now the question is: what does this student need right now to move forward?

It's a bit of a mindset shift.

And getting there requires rethinking what your recruitment workflows look like, the technology stack behind them, and how you're going to measure success.

What's changed? And why?

A few converging forces have pushed hyper-personalization from nice-to-have to must-have:

Student expectations have changed. Digitally native prospects expect relevant, context-aware interactions. A student who's already shown interest in engineering but keeps receiving generic marketing material will disengage.

Competition for enrollment has intensified. Demographic shifts and tighter budgets mean institutions need to get more yield out of the inquiries they already have.

The technology has matured. CRM platforms, AI chatbots, marketing automation, and behavioral analytics now put hyper-personalization within reach of mid-sized institutions, not just those with large development teams.

ROI expectations are rising. Admissions and marketing leaders are under pressure to show measurable returns, and personalized campaigns tend to convert better and reveal more clearly what messaging actually resonates with which students.

The trust problem hyper-personalization has to solve

There's a version of this conversation that views personalization purely as a conversion tactic; i.e., get the right message to the right student, and watch yield go up. But this isn't that version.

Prospective students and their families are running their own verification process before they trust anything your admissions office sends them.

That's the information-validation journey your recruitment marketing is competing against.

Hyper-personalization works because it demonstrates you already know what they need, which is a form of trust-building, not just a targeting technique.

That's also why affordability messaging is often the highest-leverage place to personalize.

A generic tuition page creates anxiety, but a personalized breakdown of aid and net cost tied to a specific student's profile does the opposite ...it's often the single strongest lever against, e.g., summer melt, ahead of any other messaging you'll send an admitted student.

And speaking of summer melt...

Georgia State University tried something out, an AI chatbot called "Pounce" to combat summer melt, when college-intending high school graduates fail to enroll in college in the fall, even though they accepted and intending to go.

Pounce sends behavior-triggered text messages to admitted students, answering financial aid questions and nudging them through enrollment steps around the clock.

This approach helped reduce summer melt and improved completion of financial aid steps, particularly among first-generation and low-income students.

The volume alone made the case: Pounce exchanged close to 200,000 messages with incoming students in a single summer, a load that would have required the university to hire roughly 10 additional full-time staff to handle manually.

But the lesson here, as tempting as it is, isn't "get a chatbot."

It's that behavior-triggered, individually-timed nudges outperform scheduled campaigns because they answer the question the student actually has, at the moment they have it.

A generic reminder sent to everyone on the same Tuesday doesn't do that.

Where to actually start

Most higher educatino institutions don't need 10 new tools.

They need better sequencing of the data and channels they already have.

Centralize the data first. If website behavior, email engagement, and application status live in three different systems, nothing downstream will feel personal — it'll just feel disconnected.

Tag interest in real time, not in retrospect. A student who views the same program page three times should trigger a different next message than one who hasn't. Static segments can't do that; behavioral tracking can.

Automate one high-value trigger before you automate 10. A program-page view that triggers a relevant faculty spotlight and deadline reminder is a better use of a quarter than a 10-step nurture campaign built all at once.

Put a chatbot on the highest-repetition questions, not everything. This is where agentic AI earns its keep: freeing counselor time for the conversations that actually need a human.

Measure yield, not just clicks. Inquiry-to-application and admission-to-deposit rates tell you whether personalization is working. Open rates tell you whether your subject lines are fine.

The point of view worth stating plainly

Hyper-personalization isn't a campaign type or a tool purchase; it's a sequencing decision: data, then behavior, then message, then measurement, rinse and repeat.

Schools doing it well aren't writing cleverer emails, they're removing the gap between what a student needs to know and how long it takes them to find it out.

That gap, more than any single channel or tactic, is what's costing institutions yield right now.

How is your university or college sequencing personalization today — and where is the biggest gap between what a student needs and what they're actually getting? We'd love to hear what's working, and what isn't.

El encuentro se propone como un espacio de reflexión en torno a la relación entre lo social y las configuraciones culturales contemporáneas. A partir del diálogo entre investigadores e investigadoras con vínculos con distintos Grupos de Trabajo de CLACSO, el programa invita a revisar críticamente las formas en que se produce, circula y transforma el conocimiento en nuestras sociedades.

En este marco, se pondrá especial énfasis en ensayar definiciones sobre qué es un Grupo de Trabajo de CLACSO y qué rol puede cumplir no solo como subred académica sino también como espacio colectivo de producción de pensamiento para la transformación. Además de intercambiar sobre experiencias y formas de articulación de las redes regionales, se buscará destacar la relevancia de la incidencia territorial, el compromiso con las problemáticas sociales y el papel de la investigación en ciencias sociales, humanidades y artes en la construcción de horizontes más justos, democráticos e inclusivos. La jornada constituye, en suma, una oportunidad para fortalecer vínculos institucionales y seguir imaginando prácticas de conocimiento situadas, colaborativas y comprometidas con el cambio social. Se espera la participación activa de estudiantes, docentes, investigadores formados y en formación, con el objeto de promover un espacio amplio de intercambio, debate y reflexión académica. Las Primeras Jornadas “Frente Nacional de Educación: un proyecto argentino y nuestroamericano” se desarrollarán los días 7 y 8 de agosto en el Centro Cultural de la Cooperación Floreal Gorini (CCC) de Buenos Aires, convocadas por CLACSO, CTERA, CCC-IMFC, RED ESTRADO, ALIE y AGCE.

El 22 de mayo de 2026 las organizaciones sindicales docentes convocaron al “Cabildo Abierto por la Educación Pública”, ocasión en que se lanzó el “Frente Nacional de Educación» como respuesta a las políticas de desmantelamiento de la educación pública y como construcción de una alternativa cultural, política, pedagógica y organizativa que abra el camino a una educación que contribuya a un proyecto colectivo argentino y nuestroamericano.

Los días 7 y 8 de agosto un conjunto de organizaciones, instituciones y colectivos del campo de la educación nos convocamos para dar continuidad a este proceso de creación, invitando a dos días de trabajo con el objetivo de pensar, intercambiar, construir conjuntamente las ideas fuerzas de un programa educativo y profundizar lazos para fortalecer la organización del “Frente Educativo Nacional”. En este mismo sentido, abonamos a la incorporación de protagonistas que desde la diversidad, pluralidad y amplitud contribuya a enriquecer este recorrido compartido.

Entre otras actividades, Pablo Vommaro, Director Ejecutivo de CLACSO, integrará el viernes 7 la Mesa de Apertura junto a Sonia Alesso (Ctera), Nora Gluz (Red Estrado/Alie), Pablo Imen (CCC /AGCE) Juan Carlos Junio, coordinada por Gabriela Nacht.

Los objetivos principales del Frente son:

-Defensa de la escuela pública: Garantizar el derecho a estudiar y enseñar sin recortes.

-Unidad regional (Nuestroamericana): Pensar programas de estudio y valores que unan a los países de América Latina desde una mirada soberana.

-Mejores condiciones de trabajo: Reclamar sueldos justos y trabajo estable para los docentes.

Centro Cultural de la Cooperación Floreal Gorini: Av. Corrientes 1543, Ciudad de Buenos Aires, Argentina.

Το Πανεπιστήμιο Ιωαννίνων σε συνεργασία με την Γενική Συνέλευση του Ελληνικού Ιδρύματος Έρευνας και Καινοτομίας (ΕΛ.ΙΔ.Ε.Κ.) και τον Πρόεδρό της Καθηγητή κ Δημήτριο Δ. Βέργαδο διοργάνωσαν την 42η συνεδρίασή της καθώς και συνάντηση εργασίας με τους ερευνητές κατόπιν σχετικής πρόσκλησης της Πρυτάνεως, Καθηγήτριας Άννας Κ. Μπατιστάτου, με στόχο την ενίσχυση του διαλόγου και της συνεργασίας μεταξύ της επιστημονικής κοινότητας του Πανεπιστημίου Ιωαννίνων και του ΕΛ.ΙΔ.Ε.Κ.

Την Πέμπτη 16 Ιουλίου, στο Συνεδριακό Κέντρο «Κάρολος Παπούλιας» του Πανεπιστημίου Ιωαννίνων, πραγματοποιήθηκε συνάντηση των μελών της Γενικής Συνέλευσης, των μελών του Επιστημονικού Συμβουλίου και του Διευθυντή του ΕΛ.ΙΔ.Ε.Κ με μέλη ΔΕΠ, ΕΕΠ, ΕΔΙΠ, ΕΤΕΠ, ερευνητές και ερευνήτριες του Πανεπιστημίου Ιωαννίνων. Στη συνάντηση, στην οποία απηύθυνε χαιρετισμό ο Βουλευτής Ιωαννίνων Ιωάννης Τσίμαρης, συμμετείχαν επίσης η Πρύτανης, τα μέλη του Συμβουλίου Διοίκησης, οι Αντιπρυτάνεις, οι Κοσμήτορες, οι Πρόεδροι των Τμημάτων και ο εκπρόσωπος του Πανεπιστημίου Ιωαννίνων στη Γενική Συνέλευση του ΕΛ.ΙΔ.Ε.Κ., Καθηγητής Σωτήριος Χατζηκακού.

Την Παρασκευή 17 Ιουλίου, στην Αίθουσα της Συγκλήτου, έλαβε χώρα η τακτική συνεδρίαση της Γενικής Συνέλευσης του ΕΛ.ΙΔ.Ε.Κ., τις εργασίες της οποίας χαιρέτισαν ο Υφυπουργός Ανάπτυξης, αρμόδιος για την Έρευνα και την Καινοτομία, κ. Σταύρος Καλαφάτης, και η Βουλευτής Ιωαννίνων κα Μαρία Κεφάλα, τονίζοντας τον καθοριστικό ρόλο της συνεργασίας μεταξύ της Πολιτείας, των Ανώτατων Εκπαιδευτικών Ιδρυμάτων και του ΕΛ.ΙΔ.Ε.Κ. για την ενίσχυση της έρευνας και τη στήριξη του επιστημονικού ανθρώπινου δυναμικού. Χαιρετισμό, επίσης, απευθύναν ο Αντιπρύτανης Έρευνας, Καινοτομίας και Ανάπτυξης κ. Θεόδωρος Ματίκας και ο Διευθυντής του Ινστιτούτου Βιοϊατρικών Ερευνών (ΙΒΕ) κ. Σάββας Χριστοφορίδης.

Το ΕΛ.ΙΔ.Ε.Κ. αποτελεί έναν από τους πιο σημαντικούς φορείς χρηματοδότησης της έρευνας των Ερευνητικών Κέντρων και των Πανεπιστημίων. Η Γενική Συνέλευση αποτελεί το ανώτατο όργανο διοίκησης, το οποίο εγγυάται την ανεξαρτησία του Ιδρύματος και την εκπλήρωση της αποστολής του, καθώς εκπροσωπούνται τα πανεπιστήμια και ερευνητικά κέντρα της χώρας (37 τον αριθμό) που αποτελούν το σύνολο της ερευνητικής κοινότητας.

Στο πλαίσιο της συνάντησης εργασίας του ΕΛ.ΙΔ.Ε.Κ. με τους ερευνητές του Πανεπιστημίου Ιωαννίνων και των λοιπών ερευνητικών φορέων, παρουσιάστηκαν τα αποτελέσματα ερευνητικών έργων που χρηματοδοτούνται από το ΕΛ.ΙΔ.Ε.Κ., αναδεικνύοντας τη σημαντική συμβολή τους στην προαγωγή της επιστημονικής γνώσης και της ερευνητικής δραστηριότητας. Ακολούθησε γόνιμος και εποικοδομητικός διάλογος για ζητήματα που αφορούν την περαιτέρω ενίσχυση της έρευνας, της καινοτομίας και της χρηματοδότησης της επιστημονικής αριστείας στη χώρα.

Μετά την ολοκλήρωση της συνάντησης του ΕΛΙΔΕΚ, η Πρύτανης του Πανεπιστημίου Ιωαννίνων, Καθηγήτρια Άννα Κ. Μπατιστάτου δήλωσε: «Η έρευνα αποτελεί διαχρονικά έναν από τους ισχυρότερους πυλώνες του Πανεπιστημίου Ιωαννίνων. Το επιστημονικό μας έργο και η διεθνής παρουσία των ερευνητικών μας ομάδων αποτυπώνουν μία σταθερή πορεία αριστείας. Ευελπιστούμε ότι το ΕΛ.ΙΔ.Ε.Κ. θα συμβάλλει ουσιαστικά στην πορεία αυτή με τη στήριξη της έρευνας που βασίζεται στην επιστημονική ποιότητα και με ιδιαίτερη μέριμνα για τους νέους ερευνητές και τις νέες ερευνήτριες».

Ο Αντιπρύτανης Έρευνας, Καινοτομίας και Ανάπτυξης του Πανεπιστημίου Ιωαννίνων, Καθηγητής Θεόδωρος Ματίκας δήλωσε: «Ιδιαίτερα σημαντική είναι η συνάντηση μεταξύ των εκπροσώπων του ΕΛ.ΙΔ.Ε.Κ. και των ερευνητών και ερευνητριών του Πανεπιστημίου Ιωαννίνων, καθώς ο ουσιαστικός διάλογος με την ακαδημαϊκή κοινότητα είναι απαραίτητη προϋπόθεση για τη συνεχή εξέλιξη του θεσμού».

Ο Πρόεδρος της Γενικής Συνέλευσης του ΕΛ.ΙΔ.ΕΚ., Καθηγητής Δημήτρης Βέργαδος, υπογράμμισε: «Καταρχήν, θα ήθελα να ευχαριστήσω το Πανεπιστήμιο Ιωάννινων και ιδιαίτερα την Πρύτανη κα Α. Μπατιστάτου, τον Αντιπρύτανη Έρευνας, Καινοτομίας και Ανάπτυξης κ. Θ. Ματίκα, και το μέλος της Γενικής Συνέλευσης κ. Σ. Χατζηκακού για τη διοργάνωση και τη φιλοξενία. Η Γενική Συνέλευση του ΕΛ.ΙΔ.ΕΚ. σε συνέχεια των δράσεων εξωστρέφειας, αλληλεπίδρασης και συνεργασίας με τα μέλη της ερευνητικής και ακαδημαϊκής κοινότητας των Πανεπιστημίων και των Ερευνητικών Ιδρυμάτων που βρίσκονται εκτός Αθηνών, αποφάσισε η 42η τακτική συνεδρίαση να πραγματοποιηθεί στο Πανεπιστήμιο Ιωάννινων. Για τη Γενική Συνέλευση αποτελεί στοίχημα η ενίσχυση της βασικής έρευνας, αλλά και της καινοτομίας για τη χώρα μας, τόσο των ερευνητών μας, όσο και των ιδρυμάτων μέσω των οποίων δραστηριοποιούνται, όπου θα διασφαλίζεται η διαφάνεια, η αμεροληψία και η αξιοκρατική αξιολόγηση των προτάσεων ώστε να μπορεί να εγγυάται την ανεξαρτησία του Ιδρύματος και την εκπλήρωση της αποστολής του. Τέλος, εύχομαι η συνεργασία του ΕΛ.ΙΔ.Ε.Κ. με το Πανεπιστήμιο Ιωαννίνων να συνεχιστεί και να είναι παραγωγική και στο μέλλον».

Τέλος, ο Διευθυντής του ΕΛ.ΙΔ.ΕΚ., Καθηγητής Γιώργος Καρυδάκης δήλωσε: «Ευχαριστώ αρχικά τις Πρυτανικές αρχές και τον εκπρόσωπο του Πανεπιστημίου Ιωαννίνων στη Γενική Συνέλευση του ΕΛ.ΙΔ.ΕΚ. για την εξαιρετική οργάνωση και φιλοξενία. Είναι ιδιαίτερα σημαντική αφενός η παρουσία στη συνεδρίαση της Γενικής Συνέλευσης του ΕΛ.ΙΔ.ΕΚ. μελών του Επιστημονικού Συμβουλίου και η συμμετοχή του Διευθυντή, και αφετέρου η συμμετοχή της τοπικής ερευνητικής κοινότητας. Αισθάνομαι πως αυτά τα στοιχεία της συμπερίληψης όλων των stakeholders του ερευνητικού οικοσυστήματος είναι απαραίτητα αλλά και ταυτόχρονα ενδεικτικά της νέας πνοής που φέρνει το Ίδρυμα για την αποτελεσματική ενίσχυση της έρευνας και της καινοτομίας στην Ελλάδα. Με ιδιαίτερη τιμή και υψηλό αίσθημα ευθύνης ανέλαβα πρόσφατα τη θέση του Διευθυντή και στόχος μου είναι η άμεση και ουσιαστική συνεισφορά στην εύρυθμη, αποτελεσματική και διαφανή λειτουργία του Ιδρύματος, αντάξια των προσδοκιών της Ελληνικής επιστημονικής κοινότητας αλλά και η εδραίωση και περαιτέρω ανάπτυξη του ΕΛ.ΙΔ.ΕΚ. ως κεντρικός πυλώνας υλοποίησης της εθνικής στρατηγικής στην έρευνα και την καινοτομία».
